As a matter of fact, the situation at Vancouver is extremely complex. No one would wish more than myself to operate the elevators quickly; but there are certain factors involved which would react on labour relations from coast to coast and which must be and are being taken into account.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last night before the adjournment, we were discussing the "mink coat" budget which this government brought in, which does so much for those with considerable means and does so very little for those who are trying to get by on a moderate income.
We were also trying to get to the bottom of the minister's phrase "social dividend" which he used in his budget address a few nights ago. Most of us were greatly puzzled when we heard this expression, because the only dividend that we knew we had received was a 10 per cent rebate for each dollar of overtaxation which we had paid out during the past six years. That would not seem to be a social dividend; it would seem to be a rather unsocial dividend. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that this social dividend to which the minister referred must be the special treatment which the government has accorded to the gentleman of leisure who does no work, and who pays no income tax on an income of nearly $10,000 a year, provided that income is derived from dividends from Canadian corporations.
We were also talking about the obsolete and reactionary housing policy of this government, which makes it impossible for the small man to buy a new house and for the Canadian construction industry to produce more than about half of the new houses which it is capable of producing in a year.
I should now like to refer to another matter on which the government is dragging its feet badly. I refer to the introduction of a rehabilitation program in this country. I want to show the minister how the introduction of such a rehabilitation program by this government could be one of the best revenue producers that this government would have in terms of dollars and cents, in addition to the tremendous benefit that would accrue to the health and welfare of the people.
I think we were all glad to hear the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) a year ago tell us that an advisory committee on rehabilitation was being set up. However, the results which have been attained from that committee in the meantime have, I think, been disappointing indeed.
The purpose of any advisory committee is to make suggestions to the government. These suggestions are the product of the combined thinking of the best brains and experience available on that subject in the country. The government, of course, is the
2418	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Hees only body which can act on these recommendations, and if the government does not take legislative action, then the work of the committee is worthless.
So far, Mr. Speaker, there has been no indication of any inclination on the part of the government to take legislative action on any of the excellent recommendations on rehabilitation that have been brought forward to date. On November 27, Mr. Ian Campbell, the co-ordinator of the advisory committee on rehabilitation, gave a report to the advisory committee on manpower. This report was a very pleasant one, filled with aims, desires and aspirations, but it contained no information as to what the government proposed to do in the way of bringing in a legislative program. It was just the kind of report that members of the government make when they are trying to explain why they are not going ahead with something they know perfectly well they should be getting on with.
Since that report was made, another three months have passed, and there is still no indication of any action on the government's part. It makes it look as though the government intends to use this advisory committee in the same way as it used the advisory committee on manpower, and that is a very disturbing thing indeed.
The records of the meetings of the advisory committee on manpower show a parade of cabinet ministers and senior civil servants coming before the committee and outlining government policy on the various aspects of the problems with which the committee is dealing. But it is very hard indeed to find any record of a suggestion made by a member of the advisory committee, advising the government as to what course that member thinks the government should follow.
We have been presented with the farce of the government advising the advisory committee, instead of the advisory committee advising the government. I think it is just that kind of farce that caused Mr. Rhys Sale, president of the Ford Motor Company of Canada, to resign from that committee some time ago.
I believe that this kind of farce must not be carried into the advisory committee on rehabilitation, but I feel that it will be unless the government gives some clear indication of its intention to act on the many excellent recommendations that have been put forward to it.
On the question of rehabilitation, I hope that the government will demonstrate its intention of introducing legislation in the near future, because that is the only way it can 

show that it does not intend to use this committee merely as another shelf on which to lay away an issue.
I find it very hard to understand the reluctance of the government to act in this matter, when we take into consideration the experience in other countries where they have brought in a rehabilitation program. The United States is a good example of just what can be done, and I believe is indicative of what we can expect here in Canada.
In the United States, the federal government makes grants to the states for the operation of rehabilitation programs. According to the annual report of the United States office of vocational rehabilitation for the year 1951-and that is the last year for which figures are available

we see that rehabilitation services were provided for 93,000 disabled civilians. Of that number, 66,000 are now in suitable employment; 14,000 are employed and still under observation; 13,000 are ready for employment; and just under 5,000 have had their cases classed as being unfeasible.
The total income of this group before their rehabilitation was $16 million a year from all sources. After their rehabilitation, the total income of this group amounted to $116 million. The cost to the United States treasury was $457 for each case treated, which can be contrasted with $800 which it costs somebody, either relief, mothers' allowances, the municipality, or the family, to maintain a disabled person in idleness.
The United States office of rehabilitation estimates that those they have rehabilitated in 1951 will repay the costs of all their rehabilitation in income tax alone in the next four years. After that, this new-found revenue will be available to the government for other purposes. They also estimate that over the lifetime of the rehabilitated disabled person, $10 will be returned to the treasury in income taxes for each $1 that has been spent on rehabilitation services. I believe that these figures clearly demonstrate that rehabilitation is a social service which pays the federal government in dollars and cents, to say nothing of the improvement in the health standards of the people.
Now let us take a look at the situation in Canada today.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Rehabilitation services are today provided for disabled people only in so far as they come within certain categories. These categories are a disabled veteran, an

industrial accident casualty in certain provinces, a blind person and a paraplegic. The great majority of disabled Canadians cannot obtain the rehabilitation services which they need to enable them to compete with their fellows.
The establishment of a comprehensive rehabilitation program, for which all disabled Canadians would be eligible as a right of citizenship, would involve the financial participation of the federal and provincial governments, combined with the voluntary agencies. Money, properly administered for the purposes of rehabilitation, is the one thing that is needed to initiate a rehabilitation program.
What is needed is a Canadian disabled persons rehabilitation act which would provide money to the provincial governments and the voluntary agencies on a shareable grants in aid basis, for the purpose of establishing adequate rehabilitation programs in all provinces, subject only to the necessary administrative safeguards.
I believe that all members of the house will join with the government in passing such an act, because we are all agreed on the principle that the opportunity to lead a normal and useful life should be regarded as a fundamental right of citizenship. For that reason, I strongly urge the government to bring forward such a rehabilitation act at the earliest opportunity.
And now I want to deal briefly with a problem which is facing many municipalities today, and which I think is admirably expressed in a telegram which I received from the mayor of Toronto today which reads as follows:
For years Canadian municipalities, through Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities, have sought to have supplies and materials purchased solely for municipal purposes exempted from federal ten per cent sales tax in the same way as exemption now granted to provincial governments, their boards and commissions, as well as hospitals.
Government indicated that such exemption too involved, notwithstanding that other governmental bodies and hospitals were covered and now similar exemption given on books, newsprint, and other materials used in newspapers and magazines. Municipalities now bearing crippling financial burdens and exemption from federal sales tax would provide some measure of relief at comparatively little cost to federal treasury. Revenue loss could be readily absorbed within current budget. Toronto with other municipalities is keenly disappointed with lack of action on exemption of municipalities from sales tax as is accorded to other public agencies and now publishing concerns. Earnestly solicit your support of such provision being made in budget when before house for adoption.
I believe that this request is a very reasonable one indeed, and I would hope that within the next few days the minister will give it serious consideration.
The Budget-Mr. Howe

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to take
part in this debate for the purpose of giving certain information about Canada's foreign trade, and more particularly about Canada's trade with Latin America.
The year just past has seen another remarkable record of achievement in our foreign trade. Our exports have continued to advance and reach a total value of $4,400 million in 1952, an increase of $400 million over 1951, the previous highest year. It is worth noting that the total volume of our exports in 1952 increased by even more than their value. At the same time many leading import commodities experienced a sharp fall in price during 1952.
In spite of this, the total value of Canadian imports remained at approximately the same level as in 1951, at just over $4 billion. Almost all of the $400 million increase in our exports in 1952 went to overseas countries. Thus, while our exports to the United States rose to $2,300 million last year, and continued to be our most important single factor in our foreign trade, the proportion of our trade going to that great market has declined steadily in recent years, and fell last year to 54 per cent of our total exports.
It is gratifying to note that our exports to the United Kingdom and commonwealth countries increased in value, in volume and in proportion, rising to over $1 billion. Similarly our exports to Europe and to Latin America, and to other countries, notably Japan, increased substantially last year, and totalled about $1 billion. Sound commercial and economic policies have enabled Canada not only to maintain high levels of foreign trade, but also to diversify that trade. Canada's policy is to build up a sound exchange of commodities with every country in the world. In this we are succeeding to a remarkable degree.
When the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce are being discussed I shall deal with international trade, in general; but at this time I wish to report on our trade with Latin America, and particularly on the results of the Canadian good will and trade mission which has recently returned from a visit to Latin America.
Our trade with the 20 Latin American countries continues to be one of the brightest spots in the world trade picture. This trade has experienced a rapid expansion in recent years. In 1938 our total trade with this area was valued at $33 million. Last year the total amounted to about $560 million. As a percentage of our trade with all countries, trade with Latin America has tripled since pre-war. Over 6 per cent of our exports go
2420	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Howe to these countries, and about 7 per cent of our imports come from them. The reasons for the growing importance of this area in Canada's trade pattern are obvious.
Latin America has a population of over 150 million, and vast natural resources complementary to our own. As in Canada, the whole area is in process of economic expansion, with higher production, rising living standards and increasing import requirements. We are natural trading partners each in need of what the other can supply.
Since the war our traditional exports to Latin America have been supplemented by a wide range of other products, and the area has become one of our best customers for manufactured goods, many of which are currently denied access to other markets. Many countries in Latin America including Cuba, Venezuela and Mexico are open dollar markets where trade is unrestricted by import and exchange controls, just as Canada is an open market for their products.
Our relations with Latin America have been strengthened substantially in recent years. Since the end of the war we have concluded new trade agreements with many of these countries, and we now maintain most-favoured-nation trade relations with all of Latin America, with the exception of Honduras.
In recent months we have further strengthened our diplomatic representation by establishing embassies in Venezuela, Colombia and Uruguay. It is against this encouraging background, and as a positive contribution to the expansion of Canada's trade, that the government decided to organize a good will and trade mission to visit many of the countries of Latin America early this year.
I was privileged to lead this mission on a five-week tour of nine countries, leaving Ottawa on January 5 and returning on February 10. We visited the following countries: Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay, Venezuela, Colombia, Dominican Republic, Haiti, Cuba and Mexico. The mission also made unofficial visits to Puerto Rico and Trinidad, where we were privileged to meet a number of businessmen. In Trinidad we were able to discuss matters of mutual interest with the governor, Sir Hubert Ranee, and with Hon. Mr. Gomes, minister of labour and industry, and other members of the government, and to see something of the development of that British colony.
The mission was composed of a small group of government officials and seven Canadian businessmen drawn from widely representative branches of the Canadian economy. Three of the latter group speak 

Spanish fluently, and spoke for the mission on a number of occasions. These businessmen called on those concerned with the interests they each represented and thus, by dividing the mission, we were able to cover a wide cross-section of interests in the countries we visited.
Special thanks are due to these businessmen who helped materially in making the trade mission a success. Their names and affiliations are as follows:
D. W. Ambridge, president, Abitibi Power and Paper Company Limited, Toronto, and representing the Canadian Chamber of Commerce.
J. M. Bonin, managing director, La Societe Cooperative Agricole du Canton de Granby, P. Q., and representing La Chahabre de Commerce de la Province de Quebec.
J.	S. Duncan, president, Massey-Harris Company Limited, Toronto, and representing Canadian Manufacturers Association.
Alex Gray, president, Gray-Bonney Tool Company Limited, Toronto, and representing Canadian Exporters Association.
F. L. Marshall, director of exports, Jos. E. Seagram and Sons, Limited, Montreal, and president, Canadian Inter-American Association.
K.	F. Wadsworth, president, Maple Leaf Milling Company Limited, Toronto, who represented the Canadian flour milling industry.
Clive B. Davidson, secretary, Canadian Wheat Board, Winnipeg.
The businessmen who accepted our invitation to join the group paid their own expenses, including the cost of their transportation in an R.C.A.F. aircraft. The government officials who were attached to the mission contributed much to its success, and were most helpful in our contacts with government and business. The crew of the aircraft, drawn from R.C.A.F. personnel, made a splendid impression, particularly when the mission was receiving military honours. The fact that the mission travelled in an R.C.A.F. North Star aircraft added considerably to its success.
The purpose of this mission was to gain new firsthand knowledge about some of the countries with which we have been doing such satisfactory business and to learn what more we can do to develop and strengthen our trade with them in both directions. We did not go with the object of signing or revising trade agreements or of entering into specific negotiations. This was a visit of friendship and good will, to strengthen the broad basis of trust and mutual interest on which alone a sound flow of trade can be developed. I may say with confidence that

the object of our mission has been achieved in the fullest measure. In all of the countries visited we were received by the head of the state to whom I transmitted letters of greetings from our Prime Minister. We also had the privilege of meeting high government officials, key industrialists and leading representatives of business, banking, agriculture and other organizations. The various business members of the mission had every opportunity to establish direct contact with their opposite numbers in each country. Many fruitful and valuable discussions were had and I am glad to report that while we were not, as a mission, concerned with making immediate business deals, many of the individual members of our group were able to conclude satisfactory arrangements for further business on the spot.
I intend to go into some detail regarding each one of the countries on our tour but, before doing so, there are several comments of a general nature which I would like to make.
The warmth and cordiality of the reception accorded to the Canadian good will and trade mission in each country visited was beyond anything we had expected. We know this was intended not for us as a mission but through us for all the people of Canada. The publicity we were accorded by press, radio and television was quite extraordinary. There is in all these countries a fund of good will and genuine friendship for Canada that augurs well for the future of our relations and for the long-term prospects of our trade. It was my privilege in each country to thank the government and the people for the magnificence of their reception and hospitality. I am sure I speak for this house and for the people of Canada as a whole when I take this opportunity of again thanking the countries we have just visited for all they did for us.
Wherever we went we found the keenest desire to increase trade with Canada and particularly to develop direct trade with Canada as against indirect trade through third countries. While this is something which depends largely on transportation facilities, I believe that much can be done along these lines right now.
I would urge Canadian exporters and importers to look into the possibility of further developing direct connections with their customers and suppliers in Latin America. The Department of Trade and Commerce here in Ottawa and all our offices in the field will do all they can to be of assistance.
Wherever we went we were asked about the possibility of further Canadian investment in these countries. As you know, there are
The Budget-Mr. Howe already many important Canadian interests established in various countries in Latin America. We were happy to meet numerous representatives of those organizations during our tour and I may say that they contributed greatly to the success of our mission. The Brazilian Traction, Light and Power Company of Brazil, the International Power Company (Montreal) in Venezuela, the Royal Bank of Canada, the Sun Life Company, the Confederation Life Company, the Aluminum Company of Canada, the Mexican Light and Power Company, the Massey-Harris Company and many other Canadian organizations have impressive records of business success in Latin America and are playing a significant part in the development and expansion of the countries in which they are established. We saw and heard about many new opportunities for profitable investment in these countries and I hope that Canadian companies interested in foreign investment will investigate fully the possibilities available to them in Latin America.
Our bonds with Latin America are more than purely commercial or economic. Increasingly, Latin American students are coming to our schools and universities for their education. We are interested in seeing an even greater interchange of ideas and of technical knowledge between Canada and the countries of Latin America.
One last general comment which must be made is a word of thanks on my behalf and that of our mission to the Canadian embassies and to our trade commissioners in the countries we visited. Their work and their co-operation were of fundamental importance in the organization and success of our tour. It was my privilege to see them at work and to see how fully they have gained the confidence and respect of the governments and the peoples of the countries where they are established.
Our first official stop was in Brazil. We spent three days in Rio de Janeiro, the capital, and another three days in Sao Paulo, the booming industrial centre to the south. We were received in Rio by President Getulio Vargas, and by several of his ministers with whom we discussed many aspects of our mutual trade. We also had important meetings with trade and business organizations and met a number of leading personalities.
Canada's trade with Brazil has become increasingly important. Our exports to Brazil in 1952 reached over $81 million while our imports from Brazil amounted to about $35 million. Brazil is one of our best markets for motor vehicles, and electrical apparatus,
2422	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Howe for many other types of equipment and materials. We have been recently supplying a large part of Brazil's wheat requirements and, shortly after our visit, Brazil announced her intention to import a further large quantity of Canadian wheat. Canada is an important market for Brazilian coffee, for cotton, iron ore, tropical fibres, waxes, quartz, and other products. We were glad to learn while in Brazil of plans being made for a solution of their current exchange difficulties. Brazil is giving priority to the liquidation of its commercial arrears. It has introduced a new exchange bill which it is hoped will enable them to move their cotton surplus and to sell abroad more of their cocoa and lumber. As part of her exchange-saving measures, Brazil continues to maintain strict import restrictions against many dollar goods. These restrictions are affecting a number of traditional Canadian exports to that market, particularly codfish, wheat flour, whisky and other consumer goods. I know, from my conversations with the minister of finance and other members of the Brazilian government, that they are as interested as we are in an early reopening of the Brazilian market for these goods.
Brazil is a country with tremendous possibilities for expansion. We had an opportunity to visit the Volta Redonda steel plant, the largest in Latin America, as well as a number of modern industries in the Sao Paulo area. I was personally most impressed with the efficiency and organization of all these plants.
The growth of the city of Sao Paulo is itself the best illustration of the progress of the country. This is said to be the world's fastest growing city, and now has over 2 million inhabitants. The 400th anniversary of the founding of the city of Sao Paulo will be celebrated in 1954 with a centennial exhibition. The Canadian government proposes to participate in this exhibition and it is hoped that many of our Canadian manufacturers will take advantage of this exhibition to show the products they have to sell in Brazil.
Keeping pace with the tremendous industrial and population growth of this area, as in Rio and in other parts of Brazil, the operating subsidiaries of the Brazilian Traction, Light and Power Company are giving a tangible and impressive demonstration of what Canadian capital and skill can accomplish in co-operation with the people whom they serve.
In the neighbourhood of Rio de Janeiro, we visited the Paraiba-Pirai diversion project. This large-scale power expansion project undertaken by Brazilian Traction will 

take several years to complete and will raise the capacity of one of the main power plants supplying the Brazilian capital from 190,000 kilowatts to nearly 900,000 kilowatts. Near Sao Paulo we visited the Cubatao power installations, also operated by Brazilian Traction subsidiaries, where important generating plants are being expanded to take care of the rapidly increasing demand. Canadians may well be proud of the engineering work being carried on by this Canadian company. The work is not only spectacular but involves features that are unknown outside Brazil. It was a privilege to meet the Canadians who are managing this vast enterprise and the Canadian engineers who are carrying out the development program. The company has a tremendous responsibility for making possible the rapid industrial expansion of Brazil, and those in charge are fully conscious of that responsibility. These men are a great credit to Canada and are all our ambassadors of good will in Brazil.
From Brazil we proceeded to Argentina for a three-day visit in Buenos Aires. President Juan Per on of Argentina received the Canadian mission. We also had meetings with the minister of external relations, the minister of foreign trade and with several other cabinet ministers. I was privileged to address a joint meeting of the British chamber of commerce and other business associations who joined together for the first time on this occasion. We were also received by the Buenos Aires [DOT] stock exchange. We visited the terminal grain elevator of the port of Buenos Aires, one of the largest in the world.
It was indeed a happy note to observe the great improvement in Argentina's wheat position. After the serious droughts of 1950 and 1951 Argentina's wheat crop had fallen to 75 million bushels, one-third of her ten year average. The current crop is estimated at 275 million bushels and this should contribute substantially to easing Argentina's trade and exchange difficulties. Canada's trade with Argentina in 1952 totalled about $12 million, with our exports valued at $8 million and our imports from Argentina amounting to about $4 million. Tractors and farm machinery are the main items in our exports at present. We also sell Argentina small quantities of aluminum, asbestos, newsprint and rubber tires. Our main imports are canned meat, quebracho extract, hides and skins and vegetable oils.
When we recall that Argentina became our largest market in Latin America in the immediate post-war years we should be encouraged to look for a very substantial increase in trade levels in the future.

Although possibilities of trade are limited by the fact that our principal products are largely the same, we are hopeful that our trade with Argentina can be substantially enlarged. A mutual desire to that end was evidenced during our visit.
The mission spent two days in Montevideo, Uruguay, where we had the pleasure of calling on Senor Martinez Trueba, president of Uruguay's national council, and other members of the national council. Members of the mission had a valuable round-table conference with Uruguayan government officials. Arrangements were made enabling us to meet many of the leading representatives of Uruguay's business communities.
Our trade with Uruguay is of moderate size. Last year our exports amounted to $5 million while we imported about $2 million from Uruguay. Uruguay is a traditional and important market for Canadian seed potatoes and a small but valuable outlet for newsprint, farm machinery, aluminum and other goods. Currently many items that we are anxious to supply are restricted entry because of Uruguay's exchange situation. I am glad to say that this situation is showing considerable improvement, and we hope the day will not be far distant when Uruguay can relax its import restrictions against Canadian goods. Our imports from Uruguay consist mainly of wool and wool tops, canned meats, and hides and skins. I hope that, with the exchange of embassies between Canada and Uruguay, and as a result of our visit, we may see a significant expansion of trade in both directions.
The mission spent six days in Venezuela. We stayed in Caracas, the capital, for five days, and spent one day in Maracaibo, the great oil centre. Venezuela is one of our most important dollar markets in Latin America, a valuable market for wheat flour, milk, motor vehicles, copper, aluminum, newsprint, electrical apparatus and many consumer goods. It is also our largest source of supply for crude oil imports. Our exports to Venezuela totalled $36 million in 1952 and our imports from Venezuela, traditionally much higher in value, amounted to about $136 million. We are interested in reaching a closer balance in our trade with Venezuela through an expansion in our sales to that country, and we are also anxious to seek new products that we can import from them. We had most interesting meetings with cabinet ministers of the government.
Venezuela has an ample supply of dollars derived largely from the export of petroleum. There are no restrictions on imports to that country. It is perhaps the largest import market in Latin America and imports from
The Budget-Mr. Howe Canada are far below the scale that we would desire. The market is highly competitive but still offers a fertile field for those Canadians who will visit that country in an effort to sell Canadian products. Members of our mission obtained important on-the-spot orders and all expressed the opinion that Canada is doing a very poor selling job in that country. Industrial expansion is in progress at an astonishing rate and almost any product of the type made in Canada is being imported in volume, including manufactured goods, metals, pulp and paper and food.
We also had an important meeting with officials of the Flota Grancolombiana, the joint shipping line of Venezuela, Colombia and Ecuador, which now extends its service to Canada on the east coast and will shortly do the same on the west coast. All ships owned by this company were built in Canada and are contributing greatly to the development of trade between Canada and the Latin American countries they serve. Plans are under way to expand the fleet of refrigerated ships which will help further to promote direct shipments from Canadian ports.
While in Caracas we had an opportunity to visit the Caracas La Guaira super highway now nearing completion which will connect the city of Caracas with its seaport. This is one of the major construction projects in Latin America. In Maracaibo the Shell Caribbean Company conducted us on a tour of part of the oil fields which have played such an important part in making Venezuela's currency one of the hardest in the world. There is no doubt in my mind that Venezuela will continue to be one of our most important trading partners. We shall continue to need crude oil imports in large volume for our east coast and maritime markets for many years to come, and we will thus be contributing substantially to Venezuela's strength and prosperity.
From Venezuela the mission proceeded to Colombia, where we spent four days in Bogota, the capital, and also visited Barran-quilla, the main Atlantic coast port. The mission was received by the acting president of the republic, Dr. Urdaneta Arbelaez, and also had interviews with several cabinet ministers. We had very interesting meetings with the directors of the Banco de la Republica, with the president and officials of the Flota Grancolombiana, with the Colombian coffee producers federation and with other business organizations.
Among the numerous matters discussed with government officials was that of Colombia's wheat import policy. In the past it has been difficult for Canada to supply as
2424	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Howe much of the wheat as we would have wished. Under the new arrangements being introduced, Colombian importers will have a greater opportunity to plan ahead, and will thus be in a position to buy more wheat from Canada in those periods when local production is insufficient. We were also informed by Dr. Cabal, minister of agriculture, that Colombia will be lifting its current embargo against Canadian meat and livestock when the United States does so.
We had an opportunity to visit the ancient salt mines of Zipaquira, near Bogota, and the new soda ash plant nearby which began operations last year. We also visited the modern pharmaceutical laboratories of Frosst and Company of Montreal, a new Canadian enterprise in Colombia. Colombia is a country with a highly diversified economy. It is in a strong financial position, and offers an important dollar market for many Canadian goods.
Our exports in 1952 totalled nearly $14 million, and our imports were about $18 million. Machinery, newsprint, asbestos, wheat and flour, malt and aluminum, are among our main exports to that market. In return, we buy coffee-Colombia is our second largest supplier of coffee-and smaller quantities of bananas and other items. Our first purchase of rice from Colombia was announced recently, and I hope that a more diversified import trade with Colombia may be developed. We shall soon have a Canadian embassy established in Bogota, and can look forward to an era of even closer relations between Canada and Colombia.
We had a brief but busy stay in Ciudad Trujillo, Dominican Republic, during which we were received by President Rafael Trujillo, and members of his cabinet and numerous other government and business representatives.
The Dominican Republic is one of the world's largest and most efficient sugar producers, and was an important supplier to the Canadian market during the difficult war years.^ We had an opportunity to visit the most important sugar property on the island, the Rio Haina estate. Its modern sugar mill is doubling its capacity. This project, initiated in 1949, has been financed entirely with local Dominican capital, with an investment totalling some $40 million.
Our trade with the Dominican Republic has grown substantially. In 1952 our exports to that country had a total value of nearly $5 million, mainly fish, wheat flour, rubber tires and newsprint. Our imports totalled about $6 million, consisting largely of raw sugar and coffee. This is an open dollar market, and I am sure that the recent 

establishment in Ciudad Trujillo of a Canadian trade commissioner post will be of great assistance to our trade.
Our visit to Haiti, though unfortunately all too short, was extremely useful and rewarding. Canada has traditionally close and cordial relations with the Republic of Haiti, not only in trade but also in the cultural field.
In Port-au-Prince, the mission was received by the president of the republic, Colonel Magloire, and by members of his cabinet. We had a detailed discussion of our trade interests with government officials and with the chamber of commerce of Haiti. Haiti has long been a market for our fish and flour, and is also buying numerous other goods in Canada. Our exports in 1952 totalled almost $3-5 million. Our imports of $2 million last year consisted largely of raw sugar, tropical fibres, coffee and bananas. Haiti is particularly interested in developing sales of rum in this market and I hope that some satisfactory arrangement may be reached on this subject. Our newly-appointed trade commissioner to Haiti will be paying particular attention to developing our trade with this country.
From Haiti we proceeded to Cuba for a two-day visit. Our official calls included meetings with the ministers of state, commerce and agriculture. The mission were received by the president of the republic, Major General Batista.
As you know, and as I have already explained in this house, I took the opportunity of our visit to Cuba to have full discussions on the subject of sugar production and marketing. I have already reported in detail on this matter. I may say that I received the fullest co-operation from the directors and members of the Cuban sugar stabilization institute and from other prominent representatives of the sugar industry. We had an opportunity also to visit the Hershey sugar mill, which is the largest single producer of refined sugar in Cuba with a daily productive capacity of 1,000 tons.
Our trade with Cuba has been rising rapidly since 1947 when Canada received substantial tariff concessions as a result of negotiations under the general agreement on tariffs and trade. In 1952 we exported to Cuba $24 million of goods, including large quantities of wheat, newsprint, wheat flour, copper, fish, malt, potatoes, milk, oats and machinery. From what I saw, there is still a wide field for a further expansion of Canadian sales in that market. Our imports from Cuba in 1952 totalled some $20 million, and consisted mainly of raw sugar, synthetic yarns, pineapples, fibres and tobacco. Cuban

raw sugar has been entering the Canadian market under the terms of a special arrangement entered into at Torquay in 1951. This arrangement comes to an end this year. Whether it should be renewed, and in what form, is a matter for further discussion in the light of conditions at that time.
While in Cuba, I expressed the Canadian government's hope that the current problems in world sugar marketing may be solved to the satisfaction of both producers and importers through the medium of an international sugar agreement which will be discussed later this year. Cuba's 1951-1952 crop of over 7 million metric tons of sugar is the largest in history and the Cuban government is this year restricting the current crop to well below that figure. It is certainly in Canada's interest that the Cuban economy, so dependent on sugar production and export, should continue at a high level of prosperity and stability.
Our four-day visit to Mexico City was the last stop of our tour before returning to Canada. The mission were received by the president of the republic, Dr. Ruiz Cortines, and also had meetings with the ministers of his government. The foreign minister of Mexico, Mr. Padilla Nervo, preceded Mr. Pearson as president of the United Nations general assembly and is a great friend of Canada.
We had particularly valuable conferences with the Banco National de Mexico, with the confederation of national chambers of commerce and with the importers-exporters association of Mexico. At these meetings the Mexican representatives formally proposed the creation of a joint Mexican-Canadian chamber of commerce or similar association of private trade interests, in both our countries. I understand that this proposal, which has much to commend it, is now being given the fullest consideration.
Mexico is Canada's second largest market in Latin America. Our exports in 1952 totalled almost $40 million and included a wide range of products with the main items being motor vehicles, newsprint, machinery, wood pulp, farm implements, electrical apparatus, aluminum and asbestos. It is also one of our most important suppliers of raw cotton and of many other products including peanuts, fresh vegetables and fibres. Canadian imports from Mexico in 1952 were valued at about $24 million. Canada has become one of Mexico's main customers. Mexico is keenly interested in the further development of her tourist trade with Canada, and I hope that an increasing number of Canadians will visit that beautiful country. We are hopeful that direct air services between Canada and
The Budget-Mr. Howe Mexico may soon be established and this will aid in promoting even closer relations between us.
Mr. Speaker, I have given a brief review of our official visits to nine Latin American countries. We have come back from our tour with increased knowledge and with increased confidence in the future of our relations. But I am sure I speak for all members of our mission, and particularly for the business representatives, who were with us and were able to prove this for themselves, when I say that what impressed us most was that our trade with these countries can be expanded to still much greater levels. Latin America is one of the world's major trading areas, selling over $3J billion yearly to the United States alone and buying almost $300 million monthly from the United States, our nearest competitor. I believe Canada's share of this trade could be greatly increased and our position in these markets further improved. The opportunities are there, and it is up to us to make sure they are grasped and developed. This is a job that must primarily be done by Canadian businessmen themselves. There is no substitute for personal, direct, on-the-spot contacts and relations. I would most strongly urge senior Canadian businessmen to go to the countries of Latin America and see for themselves what new fields are open to them. I would like to think that our own visit was but the first of many such visits in both directions by business groups and individuals. There is no better way of getting to know one's customers and suppliers and of finding new customers and new suppliers.
I took the opportunity of my stay in each country to extend to the governments and business groups of those countries an invitation to come and visit us in Canada. I know many of them are making plans to do so, and I have assured them that they will meet with the warmest and most cordial reception among us. I also invited the governments and business groups of each country visited to attend our international trade fair. Many of them have already done so, and more will come in future years.
Like Canada, the countries of Latin America are countries of the future. We have come closer together over the years. May I express my sincere hope that we shall continue to work together in our programs for the expansion of our economies.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the house has listened with interest to the report which has just been read to it by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). It has been a report glowing with optimistic hope for the future.
I am sure that all Canadians will hope that that optimistic outlook will be justified by developments in the future. We are not unmindful of the fact that the minister is always optimistic, but we trust that, in the opportunities that have been outlined here today, there may lie the assurance of increasing trade between Canada and these countries of Latin America, to their mutual profit. A little later in my remarks, if there is time,
I -shall have something more to say on the subject of trade.
The speech of the minister was undoubtedly an interesting and pleasing diversion for the government from the hard realities of the budget which was introduced in the house a week ago by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). May I say that I am happy to have the opportunity today of addressing myself to the minister. A year ago, as he will remember, I had occasion to complain about his absence at the time of the debate. I now say to the minister that taking part in the budget debate with the Minister of Finance out of the country is something like the play without Hamlet, particularly when in the budget one has to discuss something rotten in the state of Denmark.	,
I suppose every budget, Mr. Speaker, has its distinguishing characteristics. There are some that lend themselves to particular designations. For instance, one remembers the


1949 budget which the Liberal propagandists did their very best to designate for history as "the sunshine budget". One recalls the budget of a year ago, introduced by the same minister, which was so aptly described by one leading journal of the province of Quebec. Referring to the reaction to it throughout the province of Quebec as one tinged with disappointment, he Soleil described that reaction in its issue of April 12, 1952, in these words: (Translation):
The general note is one of deception.
(Text):
Mr. Speaker, it was thus well described as a budget marked by deception; and, Mr. Speaker, I think the budget deserved the title given to it by some of us, the budget with the false face or the Hallowe'en budget, because while he was actually increasing our taxes the Minister of Finance argued that we ought to acclaim his reduction of them. It was a strange and curious contradiction. No doubt it was something like that which the parliamentary assistant to the minister had in mind yesterday when he adopted a reference to the Minister of Finance from another quarter, namely the "wizard of Ottawa". I do not think any of us on this side of the house have called the minister quite as hard a name as that before. But at any rate, he is the kind of wizard, apparently, who has succeeded less in pulling a rabbit out of the hat than in talking through his hat.
There was a curious and interesting effort made yesterday by the parliamentary assistant to the minister to borrow from the 1949 experience and to call the budget of 1953 a "sunshine budget". Mr. Speaker, it will take a great deal of effort to accomplish that. I compliment the parliamentary assistant on the strenuous, vigorous and at times eloquent effort he made yesterday to convince his doubting colleagues that this budget had some virtue in it. But it will take a great deal more than his able and sincere efforts, I am sure, to convince the people of this country that this pale and anaemic reflection of the budget of 1949 is deserving of the title "sunshine budget". I am going to suggest, Mr. Speaker, that a much more apt and appropriate title for this budget would be the "sunset budget" because I am satisfied that this government is fast going over the hill.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I hope to have an opportunity a little later on to draw comparisons between the so-called sunshine budget of 1949 and this dismal sunset budget of 1953.
There are, of course, some special problems in relation to the budget which one is tempted

to discuss, but time does not permit; there may be an opportunity at a later stage. The minister refers to the problem of accrual of bond interest with respect to the calculation of income and also to the position of reserves and prepayment for goods and services. These are problems which I trust will be discussed when we reach a later stage in the debate. There are some special problems which, had there been time, one would have liked to have an opportunity to discuss at this stage. But in the limited time at one's disposal, one must confine oneself to the general features of this budget.
Sir, the first and most striking feature of this budget is, of course, the fact that it was conceived in political expediency and begotten of political necessity. For that reason I think that the public and this house may well approach it with a high degree of distrust. It is undoubtedly an attempt to borrow something of the experience of 1949 when, after proclaiming year after year the virtues of cyclical budgeting, the virtues of big surpluses in good times, the minister threw everything overboard and brought in the sunshine budget of that year, marked by sweeping reductions in taxes. It is not at all unusual in the experience of parliament under the present government to see these reductions and other benefits that lie within the power of the government to bestow used deliberately on the eve of an election with no other purpose obviously than to win votes thereby. If the Minister of Finance went to his riding and offered the people of that riding small handouts, of course that would be an offence against the Canada Elections Act, but when it is practised on the grand scale by the government, then it is held up by the government opposite as a model of political -virtue.
I wish to say this in general. We have already had some experience with the kind of budget the minister introduced in 1949. And the people of this country will not have forgotten their post-1949 experience. They will not have forgotten, sir, that once the election was won, once the sunshine budget had served its political purpose, then of course the taxes imposed by this government resumed their dizzy climb.
In the second place, it will not have been forgotten that the government resumed the practice of taxing the people of Canada at extortionate rates so that big surpluses were created. Unnecessary taxation was heaped upon the Canadian people. We have seen these budget surpluses year after year. We have seen them not as budgeted surpluses but accidental surpluses arising as a result of miscalculation, surpluses arising out of blunders on the part of the Minister of
The Budget-Mr. Fleming Finance. Surpluses may be a very good thing when they are consciously budgeted for. Debt reduction is a very commendable thing and should be consciously budgeted for. But, sir, it is a very different matter from just wilfully soaking the taxpayer with quite inadequate regard to the necessities of government, and in that way building up these big unbudgeted surpluses which have represented such a heavy imposition upon the people during these times when taxes have otherwise already been quite high enough.
When the minister talks about a budget surplus this year we of course cannot attach any more reliability to an estimate of that kind than we can to his earlier calculations in the light of the errors that developed in them year by year; and we will not have forgotten either that when these surpluses began to roll up during the year ways were found, as the ingenuity of the minister was taxed to find ways, of reducing the apparent error in his budgeting. And so, as last year and the year before, we saw the great orgy of expenditure in the closing days of the fiscal year, which had the effect of relieving the government of some of the embarrassment Of the huge unbudgeted surplus. And then we also saw the government placing here and there, in different pockets in the consolidated revenue fund, very substantial sums of money, running into hundreds of millions of dollars, which had the effect, not of reducing the true surplus, but of reducing the apparent surplus.
When the minister made his budget speech on April 8, 1952, he estimated that the budget surplus by that time had been reduced to $356 million. Not satisfied with that, sir, you will remember in the next few months he addressed himself to finding a way of reducing the surplus still further by devising a new method of charging interest on the public debt, which enabled him to reduce the surplus by August 8 to $248 million. All but $20 million of that difference was attributable to the change in method of treating interest.

I have the reference here, and I shall be very happy to come back to it because the statement has appeared in government print, and I am relying on that in making the statement that I have made. The sum of $20 million of it went elsewhere, but the rest of the difference, according to that statement, was attributable to a change in the method of treating interest on the public debt.
2428	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Fleming
These unbudgeted surpluses have been defended by the government and by the minister in bygone years. They were held up as having great virtues. You will not have forgotten, sir, that in his radio speech on February 19, 1952, at a time when the surplus in the minister's hands was running to something like three-quarters of a billion dollars, the minister said that "it has been an excellent thing, not just for the government but for each and every one of you." There was no repentance indeed for the grievous overtaxation of the people and the creation of this big surplus. But now, sir, where are the virtues of the big surplus? Why does the minister not now budget for one? Well, Mr. Speaker, you know perfectly well that surpluses lose their virtue on the eve of elections. The minister can proclaim the virtues of these accidental surpluses due to overtaxation for four years, but come an election year and there is no thought then of ascribing any virtue to the surpluses. Yes, it is not the season for surpluses, Mr. Speaker.
We of the official opposition do not ask that under conditions like these any more than in those recent years the minister .should budget for a surplus. Under the rates of taxation now existing it would be a highly oppressive and grievous policy. But, Mr. Speaker, we put this policy of 1953 alongside the policies proclaimed in these past four years and we invite the people to condemn those who have engaged in this double talk.
There are two factors that stand out perfectly clearly in all this. The first is that apart from the political needs of this government there was no less reason for reduction of taxation in any one of the past three years than there is this year. But, Mr. Speaker, considerations of that kind, in the view of this government, are quite irrelevant. In these past four years since the sunshine budget of 1949 the government has proceeded on its way with its lighthearted, but heavyhanded extortion. In the face of all this, many people are saying: Let us have an election every year. And there is much to be said for that; if we were going to be faced with the kind of government in the future that we have at the present time, then I think, Mr. Speaker, there is a great deal to be said for an annual election.
The general election of 1949 cost the public treasury of this country about $4,250,000. It is obvious that an election is cheap by comparison with the kind of impositions that the government inflicts upon the people by way of heavy and often quite unnecessary taxation between elections. So, let us have


more elections, more election years and more election budgets.
The second factor, sir, relates of course to our own experience with this government, because here we are not speaking upon surmise; we are speaking in the light of experience, because of what happened after the sunshine budget of 1949. Well, by 1950 the sunshine budget had faded; the shadows began to gather in as the Minister of Finance and the government got themselves into gear again to increase taxes. Everybody in this country by this time knows perfectly well that after the reduction of taxes this year, if this government should be in office next year, then we would have a repetition of what happened after 1949. The taxes would go up again, and the people of this country will no doubt be happy to welcome anything that leaves a breathing spell for even the space of one year. But nevertheless, the slogan of these governmental tax gatherers continues: "Business as usual, during alterations." The only hope of this country for the kind of tax reduction that will continue is through a change of government.
And indeed we have only to look back on what the Minister of Finance himself had to say to recall how completely the minister gave away his whole case in this respect, how he himself exposed the political motives of the government in what they undertook. You will remember after he delivered his budget speech on that memorable night of March 22, 1949, he, as it is recorded in the Windsor Star, proceeded to the Liberal lobby. And then, the story proceeds-
He came out in the Liberal lobby and he grinned, took off his big, brown, rimmed glasses, rocked from foot to foot on his heels, and then he looked across the faces at the retired prime minister and said, "As Mr. King says, boys, the timing of what you do can be just as important as the thing you're doing."
And that is the end of the quotation. Well indeed has the Minister of Finance learned the lesson of timing. But he carries it to the point where he justifies himself for imposing extortionate taxation upon the people of Canada three years in a row, in order that he may indulge in one of his timing exhibitions on the eve of an election in the fourth year.
Then, again, we recall that only a few days later the minister was again in a mood of great candour, because speaking on April 27, 1949, he said this in the house:
Let us not try to fool ourselves, even if we are trying to fool the people.
I am quite prepared to leave it at that. It is perfectly obvious the minister did his best to fool the people in 1949. It may be that the hon. members opposite feel that the

fact the government succeeded in getting itself re-elected justifies the offence they committed in the spring of 1949. Apparently they are going to do their very best to repeat the performance this year.
Well, let us look a little deeper into the comparison between 1949 and 1953. It will not have escaped hon. members, who sat here and heard the minister's budget speech a week ago, that members of the Liberal party in the house certainly looked to the Minister of Finance to deliver the goods. Political necessity was written large all over those gloomy faces on the Liberal side. They were expectant. Oh, what a picture they were! One's thoughts turned to those words of Burns-
O wad some power the giftle gie us
To see oursels as Ithers see us!
What a revelation it would have been to hon. members opposite if they could have seen their faces that night-that look of expectancy, the look of anxiety, the look of concern. They were all there. And then, when the minister, feeling that he had done his job of salesmanship, and winding up, like little Jack Horner, by saying, "What a good boy am I!"-then, of course, the cheering section did its best to cheer up the minister. His political peroration on that occasion was interesting, but it only served to emphasize the fact that we are proceeding rapidly to the eve of an election.
Now, let us look at 1949 and compare it with 1953. Let us ask ourselves whether there is very much sunshine left in this budget. In 1949 the minister proposed, in the first place, tax reductions amounting to $323 million-about $100 million in excess of those proposed for this year.
Looking at the percentages, though, we find that, as compared with the total revenue collected from the people of Canada during the year ended March 31, 1949, the total reductions proposed by the minister in his March 1949 budget amounted to a 12 per cent reduction in the total tax burden. What do we find in this anaemic counterpart in 1953? We find a 5 per cent reduction in the tax load that the people have carried in this fiscal year that will end on March 31, 1953.
Then let us look at the income tax. The Minister of Finance proposed a reduction in income tax that year that could be considered a respectable reduction, and that amounted to a 30 per cent reduction of the income tax load borne by the people of Canada in the previous fiscal year. Well, what do we find this year? In this anaemic counterpart we
The Budget-Mr. Fleming find a scant 5 per cent reduction in the income tax load carried by the people of Canada this year.
Then we will remember also that the Minister of Finance did that in 1949 while, at the same time, budgeting for a surplus of $87 million. This year, with his scant reduction- his inadequate reduction-he can budget for a surplus of only $11 million.
And then let us look at the indirect taxes. In 1949 the minister proposed a substantial reduction in excise taxes. As a matter of fact, if hon. members will look at page 1804 of Hansard for 1949, they will find that he proposed the abolition of eight or nine excise taxes, and reductions in nine or ten more of them. That amounted to a total reduction of 35 per cent, as compared with the total tax in the previous year.
But this year what does the minister propose? Well, what he proposes this year by way of total reduction in indirect taxes just amounts to nothing. If one looks at the figures closely one will find that the minister is proposing to take more money out of the people through these taxes next year than he has during the present year.
And so it is a very tawdry, a very anaemic, a very pale-yes, a very ghostly counterpart of the 1949 budget that we see in this sunset budget of 1953. But, sir, perhaps we should not be too hard on the minister. Perhaps we should say: "If you don't like the music, don't shoot the piano player, boys; he is only doing his best."

But the minister has not come before us in that light at all. The minister has come before us, again, with the pretence that he Is reducing taxation. Mr. Speaker, this budget does not reduce taxation. Let us have that crystal-clear. This budget proposes to increase taxation, to increase the tax load of the Canadian people. The load proposed by this budget is the heaviest load in Canadian history. The fact is that the minister is proposing a record load of taxation to be imposed upon the Canadian people.

The Budget-Mr. Fleming
Yes, the game of light-hearted and heavyhanded extortion is to go on; and the people are to be fooled, apparently, into thinking that they are obtaining tax reductions. Well, the fact of the matter is that the increase in the load proposed by the minister this year, as compared with the present fiscal year, amounts to $7 per capita, and a $35 increase for every family of five persons. Federal taxes during this coming year will average $340 per capita and $1,700 per family of five.
Now, the minister had a good deal to say about what he called the social dividend. That is worthy of examination. The fact of the matter is that dividends are normally declared only out of earnings. This one the minister has chosen to declare in anticipation. If the figures of earnings he put before us the other evening are not attained next year by the hard work of the Canadian people, then we shall find ourselves in the red at the end of the year; and no doubt the minister- if by any chance he should be the minister at that tune-will then apply the tax screws again to make up for what he has done this year.
In further examination of this budget and its shortcomings, a second outstanding feature is the delay in tax reductions. Why is it that the minister today brings in tax reductions which we in the opposition in many cases have been asking for for years? You know why he has not reduced the income tax previously. You know why he waits until now. You know why the government has for years resisted our efforts to have the licence fee on radio receiving sets abolished. You know why, in spite of warnings from the opposition about the unwisdom of raising the cigarette tax and encouraging smuggling, he went ahead and did it. So far as there is any wisdom in these reductions, then we say that we of the official opposition are now seeing the fruits of our own efforts. In 1953 we are at the same time seeing the minister condemning the policies that he so obstinately followed in those past three years.
The next observation I have to make about the budget is to point out the inadequacy of the reductions. I have mentioned that the total reductions represent only 5 per cent as compared with the tax load of last year. Owing to the policy of the present government, taxes in this country are still far too high. We can regard the reductions proposed by the minister as being little better than token reductions. The minister will have need of more to say than he said the other night in seeking to justify the inadequacy of these reductions. Let us recall that a very eminent newspaper in the province 
of Quebec, L'Action Catholique, a year or so ago had this to say, and I translate:
The federal government is bleeding the Canadian taxpayer white.
It will take more than a 5 per cent reduction in the bleeding of the Canadian taxpayer to bring health back into our Canadian taxing policy. The taxes imposed today by this government are ten times what they were fifteen years ago, while the gross national income is only four times as high. Last year taxation at all levels took one-third of the nation's income.
Next, we say that these reductions are particularly inadequate for those who need reductions most. As my colleague, the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), pointed out in his very comprehensive speech on Tuesday, this budget means, for a married man with two dependent children, earning $2,400 in income, a saving of the handsome sum of $1 for the present year. People on low incomes have been virtually ignored by the minister. In this budget he has shown himself to be utterly indifferent to the plight of people in this country with small incomes.
He has likewise shown himself to be indifferent to or unmindful of the plight of the farmer. I should like to quote from the daily bulletin of the dominion bureau of statistics of February 10 as follows:
Accrued net income of farm operators from farm production declined by $255 million in 1952, a drop of 12 per cent from the record level established in 1951. This decline is largely attributable to a severe drop in livestock prices of between 20 and 25 per cent, and a 10 per cent rise in farm operating expenses.
Is there anything for the farmer in this budget, faced as he is with reduced income and the prospect of still further reductions in his income? There is nothing in the statement read today by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) that holds out hope for the farmers of this country. It may be a statement of interest to industry, and of course to that extent we are glad to have it, but there is nothing in the statement that promises anything for the Canadian farmer. The great failure of this government's trading policy continues to be that. I know that the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) wants to say that the minister is holding out hope of selling some wheat to Brazil but-

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the amendment to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) which appears at page 2354 of Hansard for February 24. It reads as follows:
That the amendment be amended by adding thereto the following words:
"This house further regrets that the present budget is a rich man's budget which:
(1)	makes tax cuts retroactive to January 1st for corporations but not for individual Canadians:
(2)	doubles the exemption levels for the full corporation tax rate while leaving exemption levels for individual Canadians unchanged; and
(3)	doubles the credits allowed to shareholders for dividends, but gives no comparable credits to those who do the work that produces the dividends."
It was pointed out by Warren Baldwin, a feature writer in the Ottawa Citizen, in the evening edition of Monday, February 23, that this budget marks a radically changed philosophy, at least within the finance department, that has pushed welfare and social security into the background in favour of private enterprise and dividends. I think the budget indicates quite clearly that the voice which predominates in the Liberal cabinet today is the voice of St. James street. The point of view that predominates is the point of view of the St. James street corporation lawyer. Gone apparently are the days of the humanitarian philosophy of the old Liberal party. The Liberal party has at last succumbed to the warnings of the Progressive Conservative party and the Progressive Conservative press, and they have given us what has all the earmarks of a good Conservative budget.
As a matter of fact the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) reminded the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) a few moments ago that only this year has he acceded to requests which the Conservatives have been making for the past three or four years. If, as the hon. member for Eglinton stated a few moments ago, the people of Canada have no one to turn to in place of the Liberals except the Progressive Conservatives, then the people of Canada are in a bad way. I can see very little hope for the people of Canada

if that must be their only choice. Listening to Progressive Conservative speakers and studying the budget, I could not help but wonder how the Conservatives themselves could improve upon the budget.
As a matter of fact, if you study Liberal fiscal policy I think you will find that throughout the years the interest of the Liberal party in welfare and social security has varied in inverse ratio to the size of the party's majority in the House of Commons. It was during the years when their majority in the house was not too great and their hold on office was none too secure that the Liberal party evinced the greatest interest in social security. Since 1949 the party appears to be losing interest in social security measures. They have been listening to the voice of the Conservative newspaper writers, listening to the voice of corporation lawyers, which voices have been advocating all along a reduction in corporation taxes.
I believe the budget indicates another change of attitude on the part of the Liberal government. This is generally regarded as an election budget. If one were to judge from the response given the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) by the Liberal members in the house on budget night, one would say they were delighted with the budget, that they thought the budget was just what they wanted in an election year.
I feel that a study of the budget will indicate that, as an election budget, there is a shift of emphasis in relation to the esteem in which two different and distinct classes of citizens are held. In previous election budgets, when the party's hold on power was less certain than it appears to be today, the ordinary voter was held in much higher esteem and received much more consideration that he receives today. In this election budget it is not the ordinary voter who receives consideration. It is the class of citizen who can contribute most to campaign election funds who gets the consideration. This would lead one to believe that today the Liberals place a higher esteem on those who can contribute to election campaign funds than they do on those who actually deposit the votes in the ballot box.
Liberal thinking appears to be that, providing you can spend enough and providing you can raise sufficient money at election time, you do not have to worry about the votes of ordinary voters. If you can spend enough money on full-page advertising in national newspapers and magazines across the country, and consequently get plenty of publicity regarding the campaign in those same magazines and newspapers; if you can dot the countryside with billboards posters, etc., and 68108-155J
The Budget-Mr. Noseworthy if you can by devious ways get sufficient election workers, then the vote of the ordinary elector is assured. Apparently it is on that basis that this budget was constructed, with the emphasis on benefiting that group of citizens who contribute to election funds rather than on the ordinary voters of the country.
Of course something must be done for the ordinary voter. When the Minister of Finance came into the house on the evening of February 19, he reminded me very much of Santa Claus, who parades the streets of our cities at Christmastime. All he needed was the accompaniment of a few dancing girls, and the scene would have been complete. He waved his portfolio of papers to the gallery and to the house, as though saying "This is my bag of presents and the bag contains a present for everyone." Certainly no one must be permitted to leave the minister's party feeling that he has been forgotten or neglected, but the people who must be given the preference on this occasion axe the people who contribute the most to election campaign funds.
I would say that, judged by that criterion, the present budget is a masterpiece. It provides something for every voter, no matter how small that present may be. I believe that every pressure group receives some recognition except possibly one lobby, and that is the soft drink and candy makers. As has been pointed out already, the majority of their customers are not yet old enough to vote. This time the presents were certainly handed out exclusively to those who could assist in the election.
Yes, we get a 4-cent reduction on a small package of cigarettes. The ordinary voter who is fortunate enough to have a bank account will save 3 cents on every cheque he writes. The voter who has a radio set will save $2.50 per year on his radio licence. Of course he will pay a 15 per cent tax on his radio or television set, but then I think we can take it for granted that he will not notice that very much because it will be absorbed in the price of his set. It will be a hidden tax. The ordinary married man with a family of two children, getting by on $2,400 or $2,500 per year, will get a one dollar tax reduction. At the end of April, 1954, he can send the income tax department a whole dollar less than he will have to send this year. One dollar means a lot to a man getting by on $2,400 a year and trying to raise a family of two children.
There are a lot of these people in the country. Approximately 75 per cent of- the heads of families in Canada come within the $3,000 or less income group. There would be a lot of people saving one dollar.

The Budget-Mr. Noseworthy I presume the minister hopes that, because of the saving of this dollar, a lot of these people will again vote Liberal.
The man with whom the minister is concerned is the man who is trying to get by on $50,000 or $100,000 a year. The man trying to get by on $50,000 gets more than one dollar of relief; he gets $1,200 of relief on his income tax. The man who is trying to get by on $100,000 receives relief of $3,000 a year, regardless of whether or not he has any children. I believe that is quite a significant difference. It substantiates my claim that the person with whom the minister and the cabinet is concerned in this election is not the person who can put a ballot in the ballot box but the person who can provide election funds to enable a blah, blah, blah, campaign to be carried on, and then they will not have to worry about the ordinary voters.
But that saving to the $50,000 or $100,000 taxpayer is not all the rich taxpayer gets in this budget, a fact which I think substantiates our claim that this is pretty well a rich man's budget.
