Mr. Speaker, my statement remains true. The taxpayer with the $2,400 or $2,500 salary or wages, and with two children, saves a dollar in this budget. The $50,000 taxpayer saves $1,200. The $100,000 taxpayer saves over $3,000. You cannot explain away those facts.
Corporations in this country have escaped excess profits tax since the end of the war and we have had no capital gains tax in this country. Both those taxes have been in force in the United States for some years. According to United States authorities our corporation taxes, as they existed before this budget came into effect, were still lower than those in the United States. But the people the


minister is particularly concerned with, and for whom he has expressed concern throughout the years, are the corporation shareholders. Consequently what we find in this budget is this. Whereas formerly a corporation paid 20 per cent tax on the first $10,000 of profits, it will now pay an 18 per cent tax on the first $20,000 of profits. Whereas in former years it paid a 50 per cent tax on profits over $10,000, it will now pay a 47 per cent tax on those profits over $20,000.
The situation figures out something like this. A corporation which last year paid $22,000-that is, a corporation which had a profit of $50,000 and paid $22,000 in taxes- will this year pay about $17,700. It will save $4,300 in taxes. The corporation with the $50,000 profit fares just a little bit better than does the taxpayer who has a $50,000 income.
It was argued by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance that these reductions go to the small corporations and the small businessmen. However, according to the government's own statistics, 2-3 per cent of the corporations in Canada in 1950 earned 66 per cent of all the corporation profits that were earned in Canada. That 2-3 per cent of the corporations earned well over $1J billion in profits in 1950

2 per cent of the corporations with 66 per cent of the profits. So long as that is the situation it would appear to me that the corporations which are benefiting most by the minister's reduction in corporation taxes will be those corporations that come within that 2-3 per cent.
But that is not all the minister has to hand back to the corporation shareholders. As has already been pointed out, for some years now -I think since 1949-those in receipt of dividends from Canadian taxpaying corporations have been getting a credit against their personal income tax of 10 per cent of those dividends. If I understand the situation correctly, this is not just a deduction from taxable income but is a credit against taxes which would otherwise be paid.
In speaking on the budget in 1950 I pointed out that in that year a man who was earning $5,000 in wages or salary would pay $510 in income tax, but that the man who was in receipt of $5,000 in dividends from Canadian corporations, and whose $5,000 was all received in that form, would pay about $114 in that year. The situation for the dividend collector has been improved in the new budget. The dividend collector can now take a tax credit up to 20 per cent of his dividends. If his income is derived entirely from dividends from Canadian corporations, he can receive up to about $10,000 without paying

a cent of taxes. More than that, if he has a tax credit of $2,000, he not only pays no taxes on his $10,000 dividend income, but he can deduct $2,000 from taxes he would otherwise pay on income derived from other sources.
I think that is the picture. To me that seems very generous treatment to extend to the dividend collector. To me it would seem to indicate that the new point of view of the government or the treasury benches-the St. James street point of view which has now gained the ascendancy in the cabinet, apparently-is much more concerned with the dividend collector than with the ordinary citizen.
I know this device is supposed to take care of or avoid what is known as double taxation. The theory, of course, is that when a corporation pays the corporation tax it is paid out of profits, and that the shareholders of that corporation should not be required to pay a tax on the dividends they receive from that corporation. That is the opinion of the minister and is the opinion of the Conservatives, because on this point the Conservatives have had far more to say in the last few years than any of the Liberals. It is the Conservatives in this house who have been crying to high heaven against double taxation.
But to my mind all this talk about double taxation is just pure eyewash. As far as I am concerned, it is not the shareholders of that 2 per cent of the corporations which made $li billion in profits in 1950 who pay the corporation tax. That corporation tax was paid by the consumers of this country in the form of increased prices. I do not believe for one moment that the increased tax credit which the present budget gives the dividend collectors will be passed on to the consumer in the form of reduced prices.
In my opinion this increased tax credit will benefit for the most part the shareholders of that 2 per cent of our corporations that made 66 per cent of corporation profits in 1950 and between them collected a profit of over $1,500 million. It seems to me that these are the people the minister was particularly concerned about in this election year.
Had the minister been really considerate of the small man he could have done one of a number of things. It has already been pointed out that he might have reduced the sales tax. In his speech yesterday the parliamentary assistant to the minister pointed out that had there been a 2 per cent reduction in the sales tax a married taxpayer with two children on a $2,400 salary would save only $14.40 a year. I want to thank the assistant to the minister for working that out for us. It gives
The Budget-Mr. Noseworthy us a good argument. A 2 per cent reduction in the sales tax would, in the words of the minister's assistant, have given the taxpayer on a $2,400 salary fourteen times as much as he gets by way of reduction in his income tax from this budget. True, that would be only $14.40 a year, but $14.40 a year means a good deal to many of these taxpayers. There might have been a reduction in the sales tax; there was none.
The minister might have granted exemption from taxable income for hospital and doctors' bills. We have debated that at great length in this house, and the wiping out of that 4 per cent floor would have been a remarkable saving to many a harassed taxpayer. The best the minister could do was to reduce that item from 4 per cent to 3 per cent. We thank him for that, and we think we recognize in that action some small degree of success in the campaign which this group is waging with other groups in this house for the wiping out of that floor.
With the $100 million the minister was handing back by way of corporation tax reductions he might have made at least a beginning on. a national health insurance scheme. He might have helped the little man by raising the tax exemption level. He might have given the small income taxpayer the big reduction. He did not do any of these things. But there are one or two things the minister can still do that will benefit some of the needy people of this country.
I want to call the minister's attention for a moment to the predicament of the blind, who are still subject to the means test. Surely with the something more than $240 million the minister had at his disposal for the reduction in taxation, he could have included among those who were to be benefited the blind people who are still subject to a means test. The act provides for an allowance to all blind people from 21 to 69 years of age whose income, with the allowance, does not exceed $840 for a single person and $1,320 for a married person. The Canadian council of the blind at four consecutive national conventions passed resolutions requesting the elimination of this means test. The Canadian National Institute for the Blind has asked for the elimination of the means test and an increase in the allowance.
The retention of the means test in the case of the blind can serve no good purpose. And since year after year the minister has refused the removal of this means test I should like to again appeal to him. Now that he is in a position to reduce to some extent the tax burden on certain groups of citizens he should consider as a sort of afterthought to his
2436	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Noseworthy budget the elimination of this means test which can serve no good purpose whatever. On the contrary, it militates against the rehabilitation of all those who become blind after they become adults, and I am told that a great many of those who are blind have become blind in adult life.
Those interested in the rehabilitation of the blind And that in addition to the frustration which blindness brings to the adult, they have to contend with the fear of insecurity which is created by that means test. They tell me there is the inclination for the blind to rely on the allowance rather than endeavour to train themselves to improve their earning capacity. They adopt the point of view that there is just no point in improving their earning capacity when they will thereby lose all or part of their allowance. In my opinion that one difficulty which the means test presents to rehabilitation should be sufficient to warrant its elimination. Certainly it would be a far more enlightened policy to regard the allowance only as compensation for the handicap the blind suffer, and subject them to the operation of the income tax laws as they apply to other citizens. Why should not blind people be encouraged to improve their training, and thereby their earning capacity, without having to sacrifice all or part of their allowance?
Certainly the means test is not retained in this case because of the savings that accrue to the government by reason of its application. Why should blind persons be confronted with the choice of taking a full-time job at $70 a month, and thereby receiving no allowance, or working half time, thereby reducing the earnings to $30 a month, and making up the difference by means of the allowance? An editorial in the Vancouver Daily Province of April 14, 1952, referring to the means test, says-and quite properly-
There is no benefit to anyone from this procedure. There is no sense to it. It is useless and reactionary and cruel. It is entirely unworthy of the Canadian people.
And I will add it is unworthy of a government that calls itself Liberal. Apparently the Department of Finance assumes that a single person requires $1,000 and a married person $2,000 before being called upon to pay income tax. The trade union congress has gone on record as asking that the exemption be raised to $1,500 for a single person and $3,000 for a married person. What has led the minister to conclude that a single blind person can live on $840 and a married person on $1,350? I say that this country, with its increased demand for production, can well afford to give the blind an opportunity of


earning to the best of their ability, without applying any means test other than our income tax laws.
Then there is another group to whom I suggest the minister should give some last-minute consideration. I suggest there should be a removal of the means test from the war veterans allowance. There are still today veterans of world war I who are suffering in our military hospitals, or living on a mere pittance in the form of a small veterans allowance, but who are still subject to the means test. I can see no good argument at this moment for retaining that means test.
Then another group that is affected by veterans allowance benefits is the widowed mothers of veterans. Not very long ago a delegation from the Silver Cross Women of Canada waited upon the minister. This organization represents the mothers of veterans. In many instances these are widowed mothers of veterans. Many of them gave their only sons. In some cases these sons were their sole supporters.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Budget-Mr. Pinard
But there are other attributes of sovereignty which we should endeavour to obtain for ourselves in the years to come. We should have a distinctive Canadian flag and we should have our own national anthem. Canada has done many things of which we are all very proud. For instance, we have enacted our own citizenship legislation. Recently, with the approval of the United Kingdom, we appointed a Canadian as governor general. Many other measures of the same nature have been enacted of which we should be very proud.
But there is one thing missing in this field. We have done a lot, but in my opinion we have forgotten to do the most important thing. We should not overlook the fact that up to the present time Canada has been unable to play the role she should be playing. Canada does not possess her own constitution. The constitution we have today is not sufficient in the light of our status and growth as a free and independent nation.
The British North America Act was passed in 1867. That was a tremendous achievement, and I think we should pay a tribute to those who framed that constitution. We should be grateful for their determination, their good faith and their courage. But I believe that the British North America Act has served its purpose. It cannot keep in line any more with our progress as a nation. We need a new Canadian constitution which will become the new written law of the land.
Some countries have put in documentary form their constitutional liberties. Some of these constitutions may contain very emphatic declarations, but they remain very dear to the hearts of the people of those countries. Other countries have preferred to rely on usage and custom. They do not wish to put anything in writing which will restrict their constitutional liberties.
Here in Canada we fall into neither of those two categories. Today our constitution is insufficient to guarantee our constitutional liberties. I think every Canadian should hope that some day we will have a Canadian constitution which will be part of our statutes. We should endeavour now to repatriate our own Canadian constitution.
I come now to the attitude taken by this and preceding governments in that respect. Ever since our national life progressed sufficiently to justify such a trend of action, Canadian governments have worked constantly toward a gradual recognition of our constitutional prerogatives. This has been done in most cases with the support of United Kingdom governments. Numerous amendments to the British North America Act have been enacted.

Other measures, such as the Statute of Westminster, have been passed. This has been done generally at the request of the Canadian parliament. Steady progress has been made in the right direction. But differences still continue to exist between the provinces, and it would appear that no definite steps can now be made towards the complete repatriation of our constitution until such difficulties have been settled by mutual agreement between the provinces and the central government.
It is my duty to pay a special tribute to this government and its present leader for their increasing efforts toward a settlement of these constitutional problems. The Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. St. Laurent) has already made a great contribution toward the settlement of our constitutional difficulties, and let us hope that he will be spared for many years to come so that he may continue to give our country the benefit of his knowledge and experience as a constitutional authority. It is with great pride as a Canadian that I read his eloquent words to the premiers of the ten provinces whom he welcomed as Prime Minister of Canada at the last conference of the provincial governments held in this very House of Commons in January of 1950. He said:
As an essential step, therefore, this conference presents a very real challenge to the political capacity of the public men of Canada. Sooner or later this challenge will have to be met, because sooner or later the people of Canada are going to insist that somehow means shall be found by which complete jurisdiction over the constitution of Canada is established in Canada.
Progress has been made as a result of the discussions that took place at that conference between the central government and the provinces. It would appear now that the most important question which remains to be solved before we can hope to be in a position to repatriate our constitution is a more precise distribution between the central government and the provincial governments of the fiscal powers provided by the constitution. We feel that all Canadians are in agreement on the other fundamental rights that are contained in the British North America Act. We all feel that Canadians are all in agreement with respect to protecting minority rights, and especially those which are guaranteed to the province of Quebec by the very terms of the British North America Act.
Whether confederation is being considered as a pact between the two elements that constitute Canada or whether it is to be considered as simple legislation, I think a truth remains that cannot be challenged: This federation of provinces, which Canada
fMr. Pinard. 1

became in 1867, has been established and will only survive through complete recognition of all minority rights and those of the French-speaking element of our country. As the Prime Minister said on the same occasion to which I have referred:
That in nowise runs counter to the firm belief of so many of us that there is something stronger than any legal safeguard, and that is the good faith, the mutual tolerance and the common understanding which are the highest glory of most Canadians, regardless of whether English or French happens to be their mother tongue.
I may add in that respect that my confidence in the safeguarding of the historic rights of the province to which I am proud to belong rests with complete assurance in the true patriotism of my leader and the sincere devotion and integrity of the members of my party throughout Canada and of my colleagues from the province of Quebec, regardless of their racial origin. But, as I said before, we are now confronted with another very difficult if more practical problem, and that is the difficulty of trying to distribute the fiscal powers between the central government and the legislatures.
I wish to review very briefly the history of our relations in that respect and recall certain important dates which have marked our development in that field of fiscal legislation both by parliament and by the provinces.
Ever since the enactment of the British North America Act there have been discussions and negotiated agreements between the provinces and the central government, as is the case with all countries where there is a system of government based on a federation of independent states or provinces. Such is the case with other nations of the commonwealth; such was the situation with our friends of the United States. In order to attain agreement, discussions had to take place. In some cases there was even violence exercised before agreement could be reached. Our neighbours to the south had to fight it out in a costly and bloody civil war before they could reach final agreement and ensure a stable system of government.
This also happened in our own country, and it is in the blood of some of our fellow Canadians that is to be found the real cradle of our constitutional liberties. In Canada the troubled and historic days of 1837 preceded the federation of provinces, but they were nevertheless the fruit of serious constitutional grievances of the people against our system of government at that time. It was felt by those who brought about the rebellion that responsible government was more precious than life itself and should be the sole basis of any real democratic system.
The Budget-Mr. Pinard
After confederation peaceful negotiations were maintained for the purpose of the adjustment of local provincial disputes with the central government. Subsidies, as provided by the makers of confederation, were claimed by provinces either on the occasion of their entry into the federation or after their acceptance of initial terms of agreement. For many years after confederation there were no very serious difficulties and frictions in that respect. There were no real quarrels as to the exercise of fiscal powers although the British North America Act, in many fields of taxation, provided for overlapping powers and for the competence of both the central and the provincial legislatures in the same fields. The problem was relegated to future discussions, and this was due mostly to the great prosperity of Canada at that time.
But such a confusion had to produce one day or another a real clash between the provinces and the central authority. A state of uneasiness was constantly felt, but it was only with the depression of the thirties that serious protests from some provinces, which could not secure sufficient revenues from their sources of taxation, began to complicate the situation. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) in his budget speech reviewed very clearly government policy in that matter, and I hope my remarks will not be found to be a mere repetition of what he said in that respect.
The first move was made by the central government to try to remedy the situation and bring about an adjustment of these taxation powers. In August, 1937, the Rowell-Sirois commission was instituted by order in council. After nearly three years of continued investigation and study this commission, which had almost unlimited terms of reference, brought in special recommendations of a very drastic nature. The most important was to advocate exclusive federal jurisdiction over taxation in the fields of income, corporations and succession duties.
In 1941 it took only three days for the provinces to reject these recommendations, and the condemnation of the Rowell-Sirois report was the only possible solution and conclusion that could be reached at that special conference which was held in Ottawa at the request of the central authority. Byt what the provinces refused to do in time of peace they agreed to do later in time of war. They agreed to give to the central authority the right of taxation in these matters. Parliamentary authority was obtained to put

The Budget-Mr. Pinard the agreement into effect by special legislation which was enacted in May, 1942 as the Dominion-Provincial Taxation Agreement Act.
The only real criticism, although it might not be considered as very serious, that I could voice against that legislation would be as to the use of some of the words in the title. For instance, the word "vacation" was used in the phrase "vacation by the provinces of the income and corporation tax fields". The word "vacate" should have been avoided. Words are of great importance in legislation of that nature and their misuse may sometimes create undesirable precedents. This legislation was of great importance since it brought about for the first time the exclusive application of rights of taxation by the central government in the fields of income of individuals and corporation taxes. It implemented, in part at least, the most important recommendations of the Rowell-Sirois commission.
After the war a new dominion-provincial conference was held which lasted from August, 1945 to May, 1946. The central government was then asked to maintain the system applied during the war. A green book containing specific post-war proposals was prepared by the central government, which called for a continuation of the system applied during the war in order to allow the federal government to organize a better system of social security and maintain full employment. As was the case with the preceding legislation, these proposals also called for unanimous acceptance by the provinces. These proposals were turned down and the conference, after many sittings, met with complete failure.
In 1946 the federal government, through its then minister of finance, Right Hon. J. L. Ilsley, offered new proposals which were contained in his budget speech. The most significant part of the minister's statement was the decision of the federal government to depart from its original position of securing unanimous consent of the provinces before negotiating with them. For the first time there was a serious change. The principle of separate agreements was introduced. The provinces were offered a new deal which, in the language of the Minister of Finance, could be accepted by provinces which wished to accept it and left aside by those which did not desire it or felt they had no need of it. In those last words used by the minister is to be found, I submit, the real motive for the changed attitude of the federal government. The central government felt that some provinces might be in need


of federal assistance, while others might prefer to dispense with such intervention. In my opinion that is the crux of the whole problem, in all its implications.
If a province feels itself to be in need it can negotiate an agreement, but it is entirely free to take whatever attitude it feels the circumstances may justify. There is no compulsion. On the other hand, the justification for the federal government negotiating these separate tax agreements lies in the fact that it is the duty of the central authority to legislate for the benefit and welfare of Canada as a whole and, for that purpose, to offer temporary assistance to the needier provinces or to those provinces which, for other advantages, favour agreements of that kind. Such a policy on the part of the federal government gave rise to these tax rental agreements, which all the provinces except Quebec have finally agreed to accept.
Parliamentary authority was given to implement such agreements, and legislation was passed to sanction them as they were negotiated and signed. I must say that in the drafting of this new legislation the title used was much better. The word "rent" replaces the word "vacate". The abandonment of provincial powers could no longer be implied through a false interpretation of the title of the legislation.
As I said before, the province of Quebec now stands alone in its refusal to negotiate, and has consistently refused the federal offers. In 1947 the premier of Quebec had felt the need to come to an agreement with the central power, since special legislation was then enact'ed under his name to authorize Quebec to negotiate with the federal government. Apparently the premier changed his mind, even though he did not choose to have this legislation repealed. He preferred to maintain his usual policy of political expediency.
A few weeks ago special legislation was enacted at the request of the premier of Quebec to institute a royal commission to inquire into constitutional problems. We hope this commission will refuse to be influenced by any attempt which might be made to turn it into a political platform.
If I had chosen to support my government in its past attitude in this respect, and if I did agree entirely with the legislative enactments to which I have already referred, it was because I was fully convinced that such tax agreements were negotiated in order to attain a uniform standard of living for my fellow Canadians. But such agreements can be of only a temporary nature, and I do not believe that any province should permanently surrender all these fiscal powers to the

central authority. The constitutional issue we are facing today is more acute than it ever appeared to be in the past. A solution must be found which will permit our country to pursue its march toward greater independence and prosperity.
I listened with great interest to the constructive remarks made by the Minister of Finance on Thursday night last when he commented at length upon the great difficulties facing our country in trying to find a solution to our fiscal problems. As he said, such difficulties also exist in the United States and no general solution has been found there. In Canada the problem would not appear to be easier of solution than it is for our friends to the south. According to the minister, a new reallocation of tax sources could not offer any definite or final solution. A system of subsidies to vary with the needs of each province would not be feasible because it would have to receive unanimous approval, and it might not bring satisfactory results. The minister seemed to conclude that a system of continuing negotiations and separate agreements, a method of temporary accommodation, or in other words an adjustment as we go policy between the two levels of government, would be the only formula which could bring effective results.
I believe every Canadian will commend the minister for the sincerity and good faith he has demonstrated in his approach to this national problem. A few days ago the representatives of the chamber of commerce of the province of Quebec came to Ottawa and were received with sympathy by the members of the cabinet at a meeting presided over by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). In their brief these representatives recognized that the attitude of the federal government could very well be the only one that should be considered under the circumstances. But, Mr. Speaker, I remain very optimistic. I still feel that a purely logical solution may be found to bring about a final adjustment of our dominion-provincial relations. I think that the policy of a new allocation of powers should be pursued, and that it will go a long way toward bringing about a satisfactory agreement.
In my humble opinion the solution lies in further negotiations between the provinces and the federal government, in order to devise ways and means to allow the complete repatriation of our constitution. The effect of past legislation concerning tax rental agreements can only be to alleviate our present difficulties. It will not, I submit, solve the problem. A complete revision of the British North America Act has become
The Budget-Mr. Fair
necessary and indispensable. This government has accepted that task and has commenced it with determination. The people of Canada gave their confidence to our government and its leader. The people will continue to give them that confidence because they know the fundamental differences between political expediency and real patriotism.
I welcome the day when, by making each province the master of its own destiny, by revising and redistributing equitably between the provinces and the central government legislative powers in all fields, by reaffirming the same determination to safeguard and protect minority and racial rights, a new and wholly Canadian constitution will be enacted by parliament. We will then have a written law setting forth our constitutional liberties. The new charter of Canada will then be born. For all Canadians, it will become the first and greatest law of our land.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the months we have been compelled to spend in Ottawa attending to our duties as representatives of the people, we have enjoyed many different kinds of entertainment. But I believe the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) put on as good a show as we have had for some time when he introduced his budget on Thursday night last. Hidden behind those dark-rimmed glasses and smelling sweetly of cure for his cold, he came in and pulled what we call a stage trick. In the Ottawa Journal of February 21 I found something which describes very well the performance put on by the minister that evening. This article is credited to the Montreal Gazette. Apparently the people of Montreal know the minister fairly well by this time. The article reads as follows:
It is always the old actor's ambition to "leave them laughing". But many a time some members of the audience must wonder, after the curtain has fallen, just what the great actor says to his colleagues behind the scenes, or just what he says to himself. What does he really think of the audience for being pleased over the tricks he has played upon them?
It is hard to believe that the Minister of Finance could play the role assigned to him without a good deal of private and party amusement.
There was a great actor of the English stage who used to say: "When my audience laughs, I laugh too. They think I'm laughing with them, but I'm laughing at them. If they don't see through me, that's no reason why I shouldn't see through them."
But this is a case where the audience has seen the same play with the same actor. They are beginning to know the tricks nearly as well as the chief performer. They can see what's coming even before it arrives.

speechtext:
From listening to the cheering
section of the Liberals-and that includes all who occupied Liberal seats that night-we might really have thought that they were enjoying it; but apparently most of them did not know the kind of trick that was to be played on them a little bit later on. All one had to do, when the time came for the minister to announce his tax cuts, was to watch the people in the galleries where I believe over 700 were sitting or standing that night, and again watch them on their way out the door. I took occasion to do that after the minister finished his speech, and many of the remarks I heard would be classed as unparliamentary by you, Mr. Speaker. Hence I am not going to try to put any of them on the record.
After the members of the government had a chance to sober up and analyse the different parts of the budget, they had an entirely different expression on their faces when we came in here on Friday afternoon. All one has to do is listen to conversations in restaurants or stores downtown, or even to conversations that people are carrying on along the streets, in order to find out that the minister was an extremely good actor that night and once more pulled the old trick.
The minister dealt with the expansion of production, and as reported at page 2117 of Hansard he had this to say:
We here in Canada over the past decade have experienced a period of growth and prosperity-unrivalled in our history. As a nation, we have become accustomed annually to breaking new records in production, foreign trade, investment, employment and income. Each year our people set their sights a little higher; we expect almost as a matter of course that we will do better than we did the year before.
Then a little bit further on he had this to say:
The increased output represents an impressive rise in the productivity of the Canadian economy. While the improvement resulting from the record wheat crop may be regarded as largely fortuitous, our people as a whole are beginning to reap the benefits of the enormous investments in new plant, equipment and development that have been made since the war. I might add that the record grain crop could scarcely have been harvested had it not been for the heavy postwar investment by our farming community in labour-saving machinery.
Before going further I believe I should now make it clear, as have some other hon. members, that much of our increased production is due to our preparation for and fighting of the present undeclared war, and perhaps also making preparation for another global war that may break out at any time. Dealing with that matter, perhaps I should remind the house of what happened, because


there are many members now here who were not here in the 1939 session.
At that session I remember that in June we passed legislation which limited profits of manufacturers of war implements to 5 per cent on their investment. In August of that year, about the third week, the governor in council by -order in council cast aside that 5 per cent limitation that was passed by the representatives of the people. Perhaps they had taken note of something that was in the newspapers some months before that time, when it was stated that during the latter part of August or the early part of September a crisis was going to develop. We all know what happened on September 1, 1939. This again may have something to do with the increased profits of our manufacturers in this country.
I believe we must give credit to communism and its friends for the prosperity we have at the present time, because that is the cause of a good deal of the unrest and the preparation and expansion of production at the present time. Some of our leaders are speaking out against communism while others again in this country I believe are supporting it. I was glad to see in the Ottawa Citizen of February 16 the following:
Supplementing Christianity with some kind of social or political theory was a popular pastime these days. Rev. A. Leonard Griffith told his morning congregation at Chalmers United Church.
"There are people, not all of them politicians, who heap upon democracy the praise and devotion due only to God, while others would deify the welfare state, making it the supreme object of love and loyalty", said Mr. Griffith.
Of all the false doctrines threatening Christianity today, Mr. Griffith said Marxist communism was the most dangerous because of its manifest plausibility in every strata of society.
Communism was the most perverted parody of Christianity since the first century. "Its one god is dialectical materialism: its trinity, Marx the lawgiver, Lenin the incarnate truth, Stalin the guide and comforter; its chosen people the proletariat, destined to inherit the earth; its devil private property; its church the communist party; its scriptures the writings of Marx-Leninism; its infallible witness the will and word of Stalin: its last judgment the violent overthrow of capitalists and the enthronement of the workers; its millennium the withering away of the state in a classless brotherhood," said Mr. Griffith.
I believe those words may well be pondered by members of this house having the responsibilities we have on the part of our people.
In my opinion we have no place in this country for communism or any of its supporters. That fact should be made clear on every occasion possible in the house and out of it. I note that in my province of Alberta we already have eight representatives of the Labour-Progressive party nominated to run in the next election. I expect that similar

nominations will be held in other parts of the country. In those cases, where we have in this country such people who are getting their living here, and are having the freedom the people of this country are enjoying, I am now suggesting that they be given a first-class, one-way ticket to Russia, without the right to return. If that were done I think we would have less talk of communism and less support for it.
Having said that, I would also add that we have no place in this country for people who support policies that drive people to communism. I say that because in this country we have the goods to give all of our people a very high standard of living. We can increase production at the present time to a considerable extent. The 4 per cent increase that we achieved last year is not the limit of our possibilities. We could go far beyond that provided we were given conditions that would make it possible for the people to carry on and enjoy some results from their labours.
In the past we have used much of the production of our country for war purposes. Is there any reason why we should not use it, just as soon as we can after peace is declared, for our own people in a peacetime economy? Some people may ask, how are we going to do that? My first reply is:	Cut out the waste that exists at
the present time. We have had an example of that in the camps across the country, and particularly at Petawawa. We also have an example of that in the fact that the committee has been prevented by an overwhelming Liberal majority-

speechtext:
Very well, Mr. Speaker. Then we move along. There is no committee sitting on the number of civil servants we have in Canada. In 1939 we had 46,106 civil servants. At the end of March, 1952, we had 131,646, according to the information I have received. If you look around the different parts of the country-I am not limiting it to Ottawa-you will find people drawing big fat salaries and not doing enough work to earn their board. Several instances of that are to be found.
In connection with the 1953-54 revenues, the minister states that he is budgeting for $4,473 million. In addition to that another $280 million is to provide old age security. This makes a total of $4,753 million, and if the practices of other years are followed in the coming fiscal year 1953-54, we shall find that an amount in excess of the minister's estimate will be extracted from the people of the country. That means in round figures
The Budget-Mr. Fair
that a population of 14 million people will pay a tax of $340 each. Every man, woman and child in this country will be taxed $340, and on the basis of five persons to a family it will mean $1,700 per family. For many families it will mean much more than that because there are thousands of families in this country who do not make that amount in a year. Without paying income tax, they will pay heavily through other taxes.
I believe that we should continue to increase production and make it available to our people. Someone may say, how are you going to do that? One way to do it is to reduce our tariffs. We have many tariffs and unnecessary burdens that could be removed. At the end of November or early in December the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Minister of Finance attended the prime ministers' conference in London. At that time they were going to work wonders. I have the following quotation I should like to give with respect to that conference, which decided-
-that a more positive policy can now be adopted both by the commonwealth countries themselves and in concert with other friendly countries, to promote expansion of world production and trade.
My suggestion is that one of the best ways to promote that trade is to remove some of our tariff barriers. We also read in the Ottawa Citizen of January 17 that the Prime Minister attended a meeting of the Canadian Club on Friday, January 16. He had certain things to say there which I believe should be repeated here, and I quote from that news report:
The Prime Minister said in a speech given at the Canadian Club: "That is apt to require all the wisdom and experience, all the patience and perseverance the Canadian people can bring to bear upon their domestic and their world problems as well as the most responsible leadership they can provide in every field of their activities."
He was referring to the privileged position that Canada holds in the world today. He went on:
"This country must do its part at home and abroad to build and to maintain the peaceful and balanced and prosperous world which is essential to peace and growth and prosperity for ourselves and for those who will come after us in this dear land of Canada.
It can be done and I am one of those who feel confident it will be done".
Mr. St. Laurent was speaking to the Ottawa Canadian Club at its regular luncheon meeting in the Chateau Laurier on "Canada's position in the world".	'
He said he didn't think most Canadians realized how greatly the actual position of Canada in the world has changed since 1939. If Canada's real position in the world is changed, he said, he thought Canadians' attitude to it had changed even more.
This is a significant statement for the Prime Minister to make, and I should like to finish this, Mr. Speaker, before six o'clock.

The Budget-Mr. Fair
The heading is "Fundamentally the same".
He said that fundamentally there were no differences between the major political parties in Canada. Such differences as there are cut across party lines and are mainly differences of emphasis.
That is rather strange, because Liberals do not want to be called Conservatives and Conservatives do not want to be called Liberals. The Conservatives are supposed to be high tariff people, but under Liberal policies we have had higher tariffs and higher prices for manufactured goods in Canada than under the Conservatives. Again this ties, in with the statement made by the Prime Minister at Regina in 1949, when he said that the C.C.F.'ers were Liberals in a hurry. Therefore all those to my right and those across the carpet are sleeping in the same bed.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose for dinner at six o'clock I had just placed the Liberals, the Progressive Conservatives and the C.C.F. all in one bed, and I have not heard a squawk out of any of them since that time. I presume they are getting along all right. So, for the time being, we shall leave them there and proceed to the other business at hand.
The prime ministers' conference held recently in London advocated freer trade. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) advocated freer trade when speaking to the Canadian Club on January 16, and we find, too, that there are industrialists in Canada who want freer trade and lower taxes. In the Ottawa Journal of Friday, February 20, under the heading "What We Render Unto Caesar", we find this:
Mr. Rhys M. Sale, president of the Ford Company of Canada, in a speech in London, Ontario, this week, revealed some fantastic things about motor cars and taxes. For example:
"1. In 1952, the Canadian government taxed motor cars and trucks to the tune of $138 million. This was $61 million more than was earned by the 35,000 employees of the motor industry who made the cars and trucks.
2.	In 1939, the year before world war II, the combined sales and excise tax was $61 on an average price of $996 for the most popular cars in the lower-priced group. In 1953 the combined sales and excise tax is $362 on an average price of $1,836 for cars in the comparable lower-priced group- almost six times as much as in 1939.
3.	If there were no such thing as a tax of any kind entering into the retail price of a Canadian car (eliminating not only the excise and sales taxes,

but all hidden taxes). a car now selling for $2,000 could be bought for $1,200, and a car selling for $2,500 could be had for $1,500."
Mr. Sale could have explained also that after the purchaser of a $2,500 car had cut in the federal tax-gatherer for $1,000 as his share there would be a provincial tax-gatherer right outside the sales room waiting for his share, too. The provincial man would say "don't dare drive that car around the corner until you pay me for a licence", and later on, down at the gasoline pump, another provincial tax man would collect a toll for gas.
Those who are interested in encouraging freer trade and greater prosperity for Canada should take notice of the words spoken by Mr. Sale. We find that a day or two later a statement along the same line was made by Mr. Henry Ford, Jr.
While the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) continues to put on his show, other things are happening. For instance, we find that on Friday, February 20, the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) asked this question:
Has the attention of the government been brought to a statement reported in the press, by Mr. Henry Ford, Jr., in regard to furthering free trade? If so, is any action being taken to follow up the proposal?
Apparently members of the government had some difficulty deciding who would answer the question. The hon. member for Fraser Valley then continued:
If this has not been brought to the attention of the government, I am bringing it to their attention now. If it has been brought to their attention, I should like to know what action is being taken.
Then the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) made this reply:
I saw the press statement and I think Mr. Ford's sentiments are highly commendable.
I hope the minister will do something further about the matter.
Under the heading of "Commodity Taxes" the minister had this to say, as reported at page 2132 of Hansard:
I now turn to the field of commodity taxes. With some regret I have come to the conclusion that I cannot this year recommend any change in either the general sales tax rate or in the special excise tax rate.
The show is continued by the Minister of Finance. Other members supporting the government want to have more trade and better conditions; but the taxes stay on. A year ago last December I remember coming back here after Christmas. Many of us had to leave our homes Christmas afternoon in order to be here on December 27. We did succeed finally in passing resale price maintenance legislation.
I believe now, as I did at that time, that the people handling those commodities were

receiving much more than that to which they were entitled; because since that time, right up to the present, we see purchasers being allowed anything up to $150 on an old paring knife, or something of that nature, as a trade-in on the purchase of a refrigerator, a washing machine, a stove or some other commodity of that kind.
I wonder why it is that we in Canada have to pay these higher prices. When we go down across the boundary line, as many of us do on our way home, we find that electrical fixtures, tools and many other commodities can be bought for half or very little more than half the amount we have to pay in Canada. Today we have in the house some advocates of low tariffs. The hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) has brought the matter up, as has also the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank). One day last year the hon. member for Norquay (Mr. Wood) made a lengthy speech on freer trade and lower tariffs. Then I believe someone else spoke along the same lines in the last few days.
I wonder why those hon. members do not express their opinions in caucus, and have something done about it. I believe there is something radically wrong in connection with farm machinery prices but I am not sure that an investigation would bring about much improvement. During the last few years I have asked on several occasions for an investigation into the prices of farm implements. I remember that back in 1937 and 1938 the committee on agriculture and colonization was set up to deal with the matter. The result was that during the investigation the machine companies raised their prices on two occasions, and the government did nothing about it. We see low-tariff Liberals allowing prices to climb higher and higher. If we cannot get a committee to investigate this matter, then we should have a royal commission to do it because prices are too high. In referring to farm machinery I include cars and trucks, because today they are real necessities on the farm.
A combine of the best quality for the harvesting of grain costs around $6,000 today. With the diminishing price of grain and increased production costs I cannot see how our farmers are going to continue in business unless some changes are made. The tariff reductions as far as farm machines are concerned are practically nil. One of them has to do with plow bolts. Many people do not even use plows any more, so they do not require bolts. I believe something worth while should be done in connection with the prices of farm machinery, and I do not confine my submission to the farmers of the
The Budget-Mr. Fair
prairie provinces. I realize that farmers in other parts of the country also have to make a living.
No time should be lost by the government in realizing the importance of agriculture to this country. I point that out also to the labour organizations, because the farmers of Canada are the best potential customers that industry has. During the investigation into farm implements in 1937 and 1938 it was brought out that 69 per cent of the machinery manufactured in Canada was used in the prairie provinces. That is proof enough that industry and labour should combine to see that agriculture gets a square deal.
If it does not get a square deal there is only one thing it will have to do-cut down production in order that prices may be kept up. That would be a serious matter today when most of the world is hungry and in need of food. When the farmer is prosperous that prosperity is spread all over the country. I shall deal with agriculture a little later, but for the time being I should like to deal with the debt of this country.
The funded debt as at March 31 next is estimated to be $14,837,630,437, with the annual interest amounting to $409,456,495. There are other costs of financing in addition. This is almost equal to what it cost to run this country when I first came down here in 1936, and that situation continued until war broke out in 1939. It is estimated that the interest rate this year will be 2-76 per cent. Last year it was 2 [DOT] 67 per cent; the year before it was 2-60 per cent. We see a continually rising rate of interest. It may be amusing perhaps to some people to know that we have incurred most of this staggering debt for the purpose of fighting wars. I do not know of anything those wars settled, except to make profits for the men who manufacture the implements of war.
During the war financing, agents went out through the country selling bonds, and as far as I know they gave the assurance to their clients or victims that they would be able to sell those bonds at any time for 100 cents on the dollar. This has been denied in the past by ministers of finance, but I do know that agents did give that assurance to purchasers. We find now that the ninth victory loan bond is selling for $93.25 which represents a loss of $6.75 on each $100. At the same time people are accepting 3 per cent interest.
The minister told us recently that the government is going to float a loan of $100 million at 3-85 per cent, almost 4 per cent. That will have a detrimental effect upon provincial and municipal governments and those persons who are making loans to build homes and

The Budget-Mr. Fair
for many other reasons. The government should be more concerned with reducing interest than increasing it and thus creating a detrimental result for a large number of our people who are not able to go along on a cash basis. I do not know whether I should say much more, as there are a number of other items I want to deal with. I see my time is sliding along pretty fast.
I am satisfied that the income tax is the fairest tax you can have, provided it is properly administered. But where those who are least able to pay bear the heaviest burden, then I do not think it is a fair tax. In his present budget the minister has announced reductions of $100 million from personal income tax, $97 million from corporate income tax and $40 million from taxes on commodities.
The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), my leader, placed on the record on Tuesday last figures indicating the profits made by corporations in the past. Then we had the denunciation by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) of a sugar company a little over a week ago. With that in mind I think the corporation tax might have been left as it was a little longer. We must remember that if people are kept poor they are much easier to handle. I have a parable here written by Count Leo Tolstoy concerning the private profit system, which portrays in realistic fashion a state of affairs that is all too true. He said:
I see mankind as a herd of cattle inside a fence enclosure. Outside the fence are green pastures and plenty for the cattle to eat, while inside the fence there is not quite enough grass for the cattle.
Consequently, the cattle are trampling underfoot what little grass there is and goring each other to death in their struggle for existence.
I saw the owner of the herd come to them and when he saw their pitiable condition, he was filled with compassion for them and thought of all he could do to improve their condition.
So he called his friends together and asked them to assist him in cutting grass from outside the fence and throwing it over the fence to the cattle.
And that they called Charity.
Then because the calves were dying off and not growing up into serviceable cattle, he arranged that they should each have a pint of milk every morning for breakfast.
Because they were dying off in the cold nights, he put up well-drained and beautiful sheds for the cattle.
Because they were goring each other in the struggle for existence, he put corks on the horns of the cattle, so that the wounds they gave each other might not be serious.
Then he reserved a park in the enclosure for the old bulls and the old cows over 70 years of age.
In fact he did everything he could think of to improve the condition of the cattle, and when I asked him why he did not do the obvious thing, break down the fence and let the cattle out, he answered:
"If I let the cattle out I should no longer be able to milk them".

Don't forget that today many of our people are being kept within enclosures with hardly enough to eat. They are not given proper treatment so they will be easy to handle, much easier than if they were a little more prosperous. We should think this matter over when dealing with communists and those who support communism.
The corporation tax last year was 50 per cent plus 2 per cent for old age security and the present budget proposals reduce that to 47 per cent plus the 2 per cent old age security tax. For those who had profits up to $10,000 the tax was 20 per cent plus 2 per cent for old age security. That has been decreased in the present proposals to 18 per cent plus 2 per cent, and corporations of this kind may have profits at this lower tax rate of up to $20,000 instead of the $10,000 already referred to.
So far as personal income tax is concerned, in my opinion there is very little relief. I have just dealt with a few examples. For the single man or woman with an income of $1,500 there is a saving of $3 this year. For the individual with an income of $2,000 there is a saving of $5 this year, and on an income of $2,500 the saving this year is $9. For those in the $3,000 bracket there is a saving of $12. That is a decrease of 5J per cent in income tax. The married man without any family and with an income of $2,500 will save $3 this year. The fellow with an income of $3,000 will save $5. Just before dinner I was reminded that $5 is only the price of a bottle of whisky. I do not drink the stuff; therefore I do not know, but I am sure that people in those income tax brackets will be very thankful to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) for the benefits they will receive.
The question of the cigarette tax has also been mentioned. So far as that is concerned, I think smoking is a messy habit anyway, and I cannot agree that there is very much advantage there. I am sure the ladies who have to clean out the ashes after the men smoke and throw their cigarette butts around would be pleased if some other use were found for tobacco.
Then we have done away with the stamps on cheques, notes and bills of exchange, something that has been in existence since 1915. I am sure many people will be glad not to have to put stamps on cheques. It was a nuisance tax from the beginning and should never have been imposed. The radio licence fee is also eliminated, and I am sure the people will be glad to get rid of that tax on the air we breathe and the air waves. I am not going to take any more time on that subject.

I intend to use the balance of my time to discuss agriculture, and if I cannot deal with it fully now I will finish on the estimates or on some other occasion. Agriculture is still our basic industry. In 1952 some 20-8 per cent of the Canadian population were on the land, and they got 12-6 per cent of the national income. Farm prices are always the first to drop and the last to rise, and farm costs are always the first to rise when there is any increase in prices and the last to go down. In 1952 wholesale prices of agricultural products dropped 19 per cent while costs increased by 7 per cent.
Agriculture is one industry people cannot get along without, because people must have food to live. While our farmers are prepared to grow enough for our own people and to feed millions of people in other countries as well, in my opinion we will have to adopt the method I suggested a short time ago, and which I do not think is a good one, of curtailing production unless the government sees fit to do something worth while for agriculture.
Many people were wondering whether there would be a change in agricultural policy in the United States when the new government took office. In the Christian Science Monitor for February 24 there is a dispatch from Des Moines, Iowa, which reads as follows:
Midwestern farmers indicated that they are concerned about the drop in farm prices but did not seem to be unduly alarmed over the situation as they gathered in Des Moines for the annual sessions of the national farm institute. Highlight of the program was the address by secretary of agriculture Ezra T. Benson who introduced a note of reassurance. He reiterated his belief in price supports on farm commodities and urged farmers to take advantage of present price supporting loans. At the same time, he warned against plac-
The Budget-Mr. Fair
ing sole reliance on price supports in formulating future programs.
To me that was very sound advice and I only wish those in authority in this country would take note of it. I believe that we must retain the Canadian wheat board. I also believe that we must have an international wheat agreement, but we must not sacrifice price in order to have such an agreement. The present agreement expires at the end of July, 1953, and the wheat board legislation expires at the same time.
I hope action will be taken by the government to see that the wheat board legislation is renewed and retained as permanent policy.
The present international wheat agreement is costing us plenty of money, as is the internal policy with respect to supplying wheat to Canadian millers for consumption within Canada. During the past two years that has cost us anywhere from 1 cent to 52 cents per bushel. It is a case of the wheat growers of the prairie provinces subsidizing all the people of Canada and at the same time also subsidizing the people of the 44 countries that are buying wheat from us. To show what has been the effect of policies that were not wisely thought out, I should like to place on Hansard a set of figures dealing with the British wheat agreement. These calculations are my own and are based on figures that have been taken from the Canadian wheat board annual reports and from returns that were brought down for me in the house. With the consent of the house, I should like to have this table placed on Hansard.
