I believe the coarse grains policy is working out very well, and I hope it will be continued. So far as hogs, eggs and butter are concerned, I believe that support prices should be made available at the producer level rather than give the packers all the benefits, because that is not good enough. The fellow who does most of the work is not getting full protection. I am glad to see that the embargo on the export of our cattle to the United States is being lifted, and I hope that fair prices will be paid for cattle during the months to come.
I had intended to deal, so far as income tax is concerned, with the charging of the cost of brushing and breaking to farm expenses. In June, 1947, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) promised that such expenses on small acreages would be allowed as current expenses but so far that has not been done. Then I believe that farmers should be given the right to claim full depreciation on their cars because today cars are a necessity in the business of farming. Wages of housekeepers for bachelors and others should also be allowed, and allowance should be made for the work done by the wife and children of a farmer in the family garden.
There are several other things with which I wanted to deal but I see that my time is almost up. Therefore I shall hasten to conclude without saying much more until the estimates or some other opportunity arises. The world is still in need of more food production. The farmers of Canada can produce in abundance, but are discouraged because of the loss of guaranteed markets and the imposition of the present crippling taxation. Increased production in many

cases forces prices down. The measures adopted to date have not produced the necessary result.
In my opinion we need a financial policy that will operate in the interests of the masses of the people, and which will make it possible for every family to have their own home and enjoy the comforts of life in a peaceful world. Under the present system these good things are denied us by our unwanted rulers. Adoption of Social Credit principles will produce the means by which we can all enjoy the fruits of our labour in the best country in the world.

subtopic: LOSSES SUFFERED BY FARMERS AS A RESULT OF SUBSIDIZING CANADIAN CONSUMERS DURING 1946 TO 1949 CROP YEARS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair), in his closing remarks pointed out the unsatisfactory position which the agricultural industry of this country occupies in our economy. It is chiefly for the same purpose that I rise to take part in this debate. I am deeply concerned about the unsatisfactory economic conditions which now prevail in the agricultural section of our economy right across this country, and in the economic condition of our rural people generally.
It may be said that that is not a fair statement, that that is not the case. If we refer to the census of 1951, we find that about 20 per cent of the Canadian people earn their livelihood from agriculture. This group of 20 per cent received in 1951 only 13 per cent of the national income. It may be said, of course, that perhaps the situation has improved since then. One would be tempted to draw that conclusion from the remarks of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) when presenting his

budget, as found at page 2118 of Hansard for February 19, 1953:
The total of salaries and wages earned by Canadian workers during 1952 rose by 12 per cent, an increase which is considerably larger than the rise in gross national output. For example, the average weekly earnings of labour in nine leading industries were $54.13 in 1952, an increase of $4.52 over 1951.
In. contrast to that, Mr. Speaker, I would draw your attention to what has taken place in agriculture over that same period. The best estimates that are yet available with regard to agricultural income indicate that in 1951 agriculture had a net income of $2-2 billion. In 1952 that income dropped to $1-9 billion. In other words there was a decrease of $300 million which had come out of the pockets of the people who depend upon agriculture for their livelihood. Percentagewise the fall has been more than 14 per cent of net earnings in one year.
On the same page of Hansard, the minister points out:
While production, employment and wages rose in 1952 to the highest levels in our history, it is gratifying to note that prices have not followed a similar rising course.
I contend that is not due to the fact that inflation has been curbed in a general way, but is due chiefly to the fact that the prices which agriculture receives for its products have dropped radically in the last year. If we refer to the consumer price index as it stood in January, 1952, and then compare it with January, 1953, we find that the index as a whole dropped 2-5 points. We find also that this drop in the general consumer price index was due almost entirely to a drop in the price of food, and due entirely to the combination of a drop in the price of food and a drop in the price of clothing.
It is interesting to note that the drop in the price of clothing took place chiefly in the clothing which is produced from farm products. There was a considerable drop in the prices of wool, leather and linen, the three agricultural products which go into clothing. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it can be seen that agriculture is not sharing fairly in the progress which our economy has been making over the last number of years.
In connection with the fall in the price of food, it may be argued that much of this reduction in cost may be due to the reduced cost of merchandising and processing. I should like to refer to the annual report of the Department of Labour for 1952. On page 36 of this report there is a table which shows the increases in wage rates in Canada by industries from 1941 to 1950. During that period it will be seen that the wage rates
The Budget-Mr. J. A. Machean in the industries which process food have increased sharply. As a matter of fact in 1942 this scale stood at 115, and by 1952 it had risen to 217. In the edible animal products industry there was an increase of more than 100 points, from 122-5 to 235-4.
It will be seen from this that most of the reduction in the cost of food is being borne by the primary producer. I believe that, as a result, agriculture is not sharing as it should in the progress of our country.
This fact can be readily seen if you travel through any rural area in this country. You will see that the population of the rural area is declining. It will be seen that there are many farms which are not operated at all or are operated in a small way by elderly people. You will find that the average age of rural people has increased rapidly in the last number of years, due to the fact that farmers' sons have gone to the cities to earn their livelihood. In this way they hope to get a fairer share of the national production.
On page 2124 of Hansard for February 19, 1953, the Minister of Finance said:
For the coming year I propose to follow this same policy of budgeting for a balance. This means, from the figures I gave a few moments ago, that something close to $250 million can now be devoted to tax relief. That this can be done in spite of the estimated increase in the coming year of about 3 per cent in total expenditures is, I think, a great tribute to the Canadian people.
In a very real sense this surplus for tax reduction is the direct result of increased production, efficiency and plain hard work on the part of a united Canadian people.
I feel, Mr. Speaker, that no segment of the Canadian people is more entitled to those remarks than the people engaged in agriculture. They certainly work hard; they certainly are industrious and, generally speaking, they are efficient. From the remarks of the minister one would infer that, therefore, they are going to share in the benefits of whatever tax reductions the minister has to offer.
I think we should look, then, to see what benefits they are receiving from the tax reductions, small though they be, which the minister has recommended. We find that there is little benefit accruing to the average farmer from this budget. We find that there is no reduction in the sales tax. We find that, on the other hand, on replacement tires for agricultural equipment there is a tax which did not exist in the past. We find that the farmer benefits but slightly from any reduction in income tax. We find that he is working long and difficult hours on the land to try to make a living.
In that connection I should like to quote again from the 1952 annual report of the Department of Labour with regard to the

The Budget-Mr. J. A. MacLean average working hours in industry and in other branches of endeavour in this country. At page 39 of this annual report there is this to be found:
The average normal work week for plant workers in Canadian manufacturing was 43-6 in October, 1951. This is a decrease of about 2 hours since 1947. More than one-third of the plant workers in 1951 were on a 40-hour week as compared with a proportion of less than one-fifth in 1947. To a large extent, the shortening has been effected by the elimination of Saturday work, about 70 per cent of the plant employees in manufacturing being on a 5-day week by October, 1951 as compared with about 50 per cent in 1947.
A similar, although more gradual, trend is seen in the figures for office employees whose work schedule is generally less than that for those in the plant. In 1951, the average for these workers in manufacturing was 38-6. In recent years, the proportion of office workers on a 371-hour week has increased sharply. About half the office workers in manufacturing were on a work schedule of 371 hours or less in 1951. More than three-quarters of the office employees were on a five-day week.
Mr. Speaker, there is no such thing as a five-day week in agriculture. On most farms the farmer works not five or six days but seven days a week. From that point of view I think it is most unfair to take the attitude that those engaged in agriculture should not share in any benefits which are going because they do not work long enough hours. Having read this quotation from the annual report of the Department of Labour I could say that, generally speaking, the agricultural worker works more than 37 hours a week. If I said that, I think it would be perhaps the greatest understatement of the year, because I personally know that most farmers work that many hours in three days.
In any case, the resulting situation in which the agricultural industry finds itself is that the economy of rural Canada is deteriorating. There is hardly a rural area in this country that is not finding it difficult to maintain itself. People will explain this away by saying, "Well, the economic agricultural unit is now larger; therefore each family must operate a much larger farm in order to make it economically feasible", the same as is done in Russia, only on a slightly different basis.
That factor alone does not explain the situation, because the efficiency of agriculture has increased rapidly in the last number of years. Agricultural costs have also increased, but the prices received by agriculture are now declining. Our industry finds itself ground between the upper and the nether millstones. It finds itself caught between rising costs on the one hand and lowering prices for what it has to sell on the other.
The result is that more and more farms in this country, especially in the maritimes, 

are becoming vacant; and in spite of the patent benefits there are to be derived from living in the country, more and more people are forced to give up farming and to earn their livelihood in some other way. Every family unit which becomes vacant in the country makes it that much more difficult for those who remain to make a reasonable livelihood, and that much more difficult for the community to support schools, churches, roads, power lines, telephone lines and all the other benefits which it is only right that rural people should have as well as those who live in urban centres.
It may be argued that the agricultural industry has been looked after, as far as this budget is concerned, by the reduction in the individual income tax. I think that argument is worthy of a second look. If you consider the average farmer as being married and having two children, it would be necessary for him to have an annual income of more than $2,300 a year to benefit from the reductions in personal income tax which have been made in this budget. If his income is $2,400 in 1953, he will benefit for the whole year to the extent of $1, which is less than a third of a cent a day for 1953. You may say that he benefits from the reduction of four cents a package in the tax on cigarettes. Mr. Speaker, most farmers that I know either smoke a pipe or roll their own. They cannot afford to smoke ready-made cigarettes.
I was interested to find some specific cases of how this budget might apply to a typical rural area, and I took the rural part of the riding which I represent as perhaps being typical of a rural area in the maritime provinces. I found that in a rural population of' about 25,000 people in 1950, there were at that time only 340 people earning enough income to be taxable. Although I have no figures to prove it, I suspect that the number who will earn a taxable income in 1953 will be even smaller. It therefore follows that of the 25,000 rural people in Queens county,, only about 340 will benefit in any way from the tax reductions which the minister has made in his budget.
I was greatly interested in a statement which the minister made in his budget speech, apparently with considerable satisfaction, after he gave a table which indicated our net debt, our per capita net debt and our net debt as a percentage of gross national product. The minister said, as reported at page 2122 of Hansard:
I commend this table to the attention of hon. members who will see that while our total net debt has declined by 17 per cent since 1946, the per-capita debt has fallen from $1,092 to $752 or 31 per cent. In 1939 our net debt was equal to 60 per-

cent of our gross national product for that year, in 1946 it was 113 per cent of our gross national product, and it now stands at only 48 per cent. To put it in more realistic terms, our 1939 debt represented 31 weeks of the nation's output, in 1946 it was about 60 weeks, but today's debt could be covered by the product of 25 weeks' work. The real burden of our debt has been considerably more than halved over the past 7 years.
I do not quite understand that statement, because I believe the minister is either fooling himself or trying to fool everyone else when he makes it. He knows as well as the average person that this is a world in which a person gets nothing for nothing, and this is also a country in which at the present time you get very little for a dollar. This is a world where in the main you cannot get something for nothing. If our national debt has in effect been halved by this sort of thing, someone has paid it.
I do not argue that it has not been reduced, but I do maintain that the people who have reduced it are the people who in good faith bought victory bonds from their savings during the war years when much of this debt was accumulated. They invested their hard-earned savings in bonds measured in dollars of that day, and they will be repaid in dollars of the present time which have less than half the purchasing power of the dollars they gave for the bonds. In effect, that is how our national debt has been reduced. We have a situation where the people who contributed their hard-earned savings during the war contributed dollars which had real purchasing power, and they will be paid back with about half that amount of purchasing power. That I believe is one of the reasons there is a tendency for interest rates to rise.
People realize that they have two choices. If this inflation keeps on, they are much better advised to invest their savings in real property than in bonds or anything of that sort. In order to be induced to invest in bonds they must be rewarded by a relatively high interest rate, because they have seen what has happened to investments they made during the war. They are not even cashable at face value at the present time; and even if they were, their purchasing power, or what they would receive for them, would be only about half the purchasing power that they paid in for those bonds.
It may be said "Well, what is the matter with that? That is quite all right". I should like to recall, Mr. Speaker, that after the first world war Germany paid off its national debt entirely by the process of inflation. But instead of pulling just one rabbit out of the hat and creating a 50 per cent inflation, the Germans after the first world war pulled both rabbits out of the hat and inflated their
The Budget-Mr. J. A. MacLean money to such an extent that it was worthless, so that their national debt had no meaning. If the Minister of Finance has any notion of pulling another rabbit out of the hat in the way of inflation to reduce the national debt further I would recommend to him that before doing so he think very carefully of the effects of inflation and of the habits of rabbits.
There is another aspect of this budget in which the people of Canada find cold comfort, namely the position of people on fixed incomes. Their position is a corollary of that about which I have been speaking. It is due to the fact that inflation has taken place in this country. People on fixed incomes find that their present income has only approximately half the purchasing power of their income of seven or eight years ago, and they are in a most difficult position. This applies to people who are living on proceeds of insurance policies, to people who are in receipt of pensions and all types of fixed incomes.
In connection with the reduction of income tax on corporations, there is one aspect with which I am anything but pleased. I refer to the fact that no special consideration has been given to corporations whose business it is to provide public utilities to the public generally. That is a very real problem in the province from which I come, because in that province both telephone service and electric power are distributed by private corporations who are forced to pay income tax from their profits. As a result of that, the consumers of the electric power and of the services that these public utilities provide are subject to an indirect taxation which does not fall on people living in other provinces where these facilities are provided by provincial crown corporations and co-operatives. This is something that I should like again to bring to the attention of the Minister of Finance because it is creating a real hardship in my province, especially as far as rural electrification is concerned.
In addition to what I have already said, when I see that there has been no reduction in sales tax-and that is the only way a fair and equitable benefit could be given to people in the lower income brackets, and to farmers and labourers and people whose income is not taxable-I have a further observation to make. I note that municipalities and cities across this country are forced to pay sales tax on equipment of a type which is exempt from sales tax when purchased by a provincial government. To me that seems to be a very unfair state of affairs. I hold in my

The Budget-Mr. Major hand a letter from the council of a city in this country, which reads in part:
Our city, in common probably with all other cities in Canada, feels strongly that, being a local government responsible for a limited area and obliged to expend the citizens' money for purchases similar to those made by provincial governments, it should have the same favourable exemption as that accorded to provincial governments. Indisputably, it spends public money for public good and the discrimination is beyond understanding.
I must say that as far as I am concerned this discrimination is beyond understanding. I recognize that there would be difficulties in administration, but I am sure that if it was given careful study some means could be found to circumvent any very great difficulties as far as administration was concerned.
It would be unfair if I were to suggest that there is nothing right with this budget. After all, I imagine there was never a budget in which there was not something good. In that connection I should like to make a brief reference to the fact that the radio licence fee has been abolished. I believe that is an unadulterated good. I am delighted, too, that the nuisance tax on cheques has been eliminated. These are two nuisance taxes, the costs of collection of which were very high. Their nuisance value was much beyond their real value, and I am delighted to see both of them go.
The budget speech was extremely well delivered, and in it I have noted another paragraph with which I can agree most heartily. The minister says:
Tax laws should avoid placing too great a penalty on successful effort. Every reasonable incentive should be given to people to work hard, move to better-paid jobs, take risks and expand their businesses without keeping one eye continually on the tax-gatherer. This is particularly important in a growing and expanding country such as ours where there is so much to be accomplished.
I think that statement expresses in a very fine way the principles for which the party to which I belong stands, and I am delighted to see those sentiments expressed by the minister.
Looking at these three last observations in the budget, one might be tempted to conclude that the government has recognized the benefits which would accrue to the country if we had a Conservative government. One might see in these portions of the budget an attempt-a feeble attempt, X admit-nevertheless an attempt to give the country a Conservative government by process of evolution, rather than by process of election.

subtopic: LOSSES SUFFERED BY FARMERS AS A RESULT OF SUBSIDIZING CANADIAN CONSUMERS DURING 1946 TO 1949 CROP YEARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I take this opportunity to bring to your


attention some of the problems that are of much concern to the farm producers and the consumers of my district.
I would first like to commend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) for the careful consideration he has used in applying the various tax reductions, while at the same time appraising his revenue with a view to budgeting for a safe balance. Personally I have always believed in the principle of a budget that provided for a surplus to take care of the public debt. Along with careful expenditure it was always my conviction that the decrease of interest payments, through the reduction of public obligations, was one of the sane ways to reduce taxation.
Of course I would not think of a surplus acquired by overtaxation; but when a greater national expansion permits a surplus without increasing tax rates, then I would surely welcome it, and apply it toward the reduction of our national debt. I know most of us would prefer not to have to pay taxes, but it is impossible to have services and social security without them. Those of us who went through the thirties remember our difficulty in paying limited taxes at that time, and I am sure we would not trade our buoyancy and taxes of today for the debts incurred and the depression of that day.
May I now say that most of the people of my county are dependent upon agriculture for their income. Our towns are also largely dependent upon the farm income for their business. The prosperity of our farmers depends solely upon the prices realized for their products, and by the same token the people of our towns depend largely upon the purchasing power of the farmer. You can therefore see why the progress of the one is largely responsible for the progress of the other.
Perhaps I should again bring to your attention the fact that, unlike industrial production, which is timed and controlled by the will of man, farm production is largely controlled by the will of nature. Conscious of the food requirements of his country, the farm producer must always plan for more than the immediate requirements, to make sure that his fellow citizen and consumer has enough at all times. If in hisi endeavour to supply his fellow citizen he must produce more than the immediate requirement, then surely he should not be asked further to tighten his belt and bear alone the full burden of a food cheaper in price than what it actually takes to produce it. I would think this responsibility should be borne jointly by both the producer and his fellow citizen.
We know that industrial controlled production reckons wages and costs in setting

up the sale and resale price of the manufactured article. Would it be advantageous to the consumer if the farmer were to recommend the discontinuance of the present price support and subsidy principle, and were to adopt the industrial system of controlled production, together with prices that would include the consideration of services and other costs in setting the price of the farm product?
In protecting the interest of both the consumer and producer I would like to commend the government for the support it has given our farm products under the Agricultural Prices Support Act when the necessity arose. These support prices, though not always at a level that the producer would like to see, nevertheless have the effect of preventing the producer from losing more than he otherwise would, if no support were given. At the same time the consumer is saved from eventually paying the considerably higher price which would result if production was allowed to decline to where it would go, should no support be given.
The present policy of applying support prices has the effect of avoiding extremes in production, and at the same time protecting the price both to the consumer and the farmer. I also believe that the government's aim should be toward the application of a policy that would encourage more stability both as to production and price, a policy that would diminish the causes leading to periods of extremely high or low production followed by wide variations in price. Towards this end, perhaps our Canadian federation of agriculture, working with the bureau of statistics, could be of assistance in directing a balanced production, which would allow for a more stabilized price at all times.
The over-all picture of farm income may show that the national income of Canadian farms in 1952 is just as high as or higher than the previous year. However, it must be remembered that in western Canada a bumper crop was harvested along with half of the 1951 crop harvested in the spring. This being so, and with the total farm income equal to the previous year, it is equally apparent that the income of the farms of eastern Canada was decreased by a proportionate amount.
While the prices of livestock, cheese, poultry and eggs declined by an average of from 15 to 30 per cent in 1952, figures released by the bureau of statistics inform us that wages throughout Canada were increased by approximately 12 per cent. From these figures we can reasonably assume a corresponding increase in the price of goods and supplies that the farmers must
The Budget-Mr. Major purchase. At the same time I think it should be reasonable and fair to expect a corresponding and related increase in the prices of the products he must sell.
Should it be desirable to keep the price to the consumer at a level lower than the actual cost to the producer without applying support, then the only alternative would be to apply a subsidy at the consumer level to take care of the rising production cost, and at the same time not pass it on to the consumer. As the extent of the drop in production has a close relation to the amount of support given when prices axe depressed, the support program as applied to cattle, hogs, eggs, cheese and butter should be sufficient to arrest the production hesitancy caused by the depressed price.
In eastern Canada we depend a great deal on the sale of our surplus dairy cattle to the United States. As a result of the embargo following the foot-and-mouth outbreak these dairy cattle, for the most part, had to be retained on the farms. At the same time Great Britain did not renew her cheese contract, and on top of this New Zealand cheese was being imported by the trade. These cheese milk producers found themselves without an outlet and the cheese factory owner was also greatly disturbed as he could see his life earnings disappear with his cheese factory.
I wish to thank the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) for his endeavour to clear the situation that existed at that time. I am sure the farmers of eastern Canada are highly appreciative of the fact that the federal government lost no time in entering into an agreement with the government of New Zealand to have imports of New Zealand cheese discontinued. May I also tender my appreciation both to the federal and Ontario governments; to the federal government for its assistance and co-operation in setting up the cheese producers, through the Ontario marketing board under the federal co-operative marketing act, with a guaranteed price of 80 per cent of the average of the last three years, and to the provincial government for their further guarantee to bring it up to the full 100 per cent of the average of the last three years.
To avoid the recurrence of conditions such as we experienced last year, I would suggest that more consideration be given to a system of government permits when the importation of dairy products becomes necessary to keep a proper balance between dairy production and supply.
There is another matter that I would like to deal with; that is the contention that the

The Budget-Mr. Major answer to the problems of dairying and farming generally lies not in higher prices for the product but in efficient production and lower costs proportioned to the needs of the consumer and outside markets. The looseness with which this expression is used often creates the impression that the dairy producer is inefficient, doing his work haphazardly and without method or calculation. If the farmer of frontier days could get along without very careful planning or the keeping of books let me assure you, Mr. Speaker, that the income tax department has made the farmer of today very alert to the keeping of records of his sales and costs as well as all other data that are of assistance to him in the planning of his production.
When we speak of efficient production we should not lose sight of the fact that the farm producer is continually striving, to increase his efficiency, and in addition to his own efforts he is strongly aided by the experimental farms, who are continually searching for ways leading to better yields and more efficient methods of produotion. The operation of a dairy or mixed farm requires the use of constant and applied labour; and when prices obtained for farm products are not sufficient to realize a net equal to that which can be obtained by other employment, then farms are vacated.
With the disappearance of low-wage labour and the depletion of our farm population, those remaining on the farms have to resort to more mechanization and hydro installations if they wish the production quota to be continued; but this does not necessarily mean a cheaper production. On the contrary the initial cost, together with repair and maintenance of the increased equipment, tends to offset the advantage that we otherwise gain. Of course unless increased efficiency, newer methods or increased mechanization reduce production costs they are of no benefit to the producer or consumer in so far as price is concerned.
While efficiency may play a small part in the over-all cost of production it must be noted that the main cost is made up of feed, equipment and services that go into the farm product. It must also be remembered that the producer has no control over the latter, and they are the main part that must be reckoned with when the farmer strives to reduce his production cost.
We should also keep in mind that the farmer's week is one of 70 hours or more and that he receives the gratuitous labour of his wife and family, which the wife gives by taking extra hours to do her housework. It is therefore quite impossible for him, for the most part, to reduce his production cost from


the standpoint of labour. Unless the cost price of the essentials which he has to buy such as feed, machinery, equipment and services be reduced, how can you expect him to reduce his over-all production cost?
There is also another matter which causes great concern to my constituents, and that is the inroad of synthetic foods which are a serious threat to the dairy industry. The preparation and manufacture of these synthetic foods give employment to very few people. On the other hand the dairy industry employs a larger number of our population. If these synthetic inroads are allowed to continue and increase they will seriously jeopardize the dairy industry. The dairy farm population is one of our good and steady markets for Canadian manufactured products.
As long as our dairy farmer is assured of a market for his dairy products at fair and reasonable prices he will be in a position to buy Canadian manufactured products. This in turn will assure work to Canadian labour in our factories. Unless something is done and done quickly to arrest the inroads of these synthetic products, the sales of our dairy products and the purchasing power of our dairy farmers will be greatly reduced. This in turn will force the dairy farmer to limit his purchases of equipment and essential needs, with the result that Canadian employment will be greatly affected through overfilled warehouses and lay-offs.
I know very little of these synthetic foods but I have in my possession a Shur-Gain bulletin, dated Montreal, January 15, 1951, which deals with synthetics as compared to animal proteins in the preparation of feeds for our baby chicks, and I quote:
A.P.F., animal protein factor, vitamin B 12, these things have received a great deal of publicity during the past few months.
Extravagant claims for some of these synthetics have been made. After a few months background of testing, the smoke has cleared somewhat and the true picture has emerged. A.P.F. supplement is no substitute for natural animal protein such as meat meal, fish meal, milk powder.
It goes on with further details.
Now, if these animal protein factor supplements or synthetics are no substitute for animal protein to be used in the preparation of feed for our baby chicks, surely they should not substitute for animal protein as contained in milk, ice cream or other products for our Canadian babies, children or adults.
If we are to protect our dairy farmers from synthetic inroads we know that the first responsibility lies with the provincial governments, in whom the supreme court has vested the responsibility. Following the decision by the supreme court, the provinces of

Quebec and Prince Edward Island immediately enacted legislation to deal with the problem within their respective borders. The province of Ontario passed an act respecting edible oil products which was assented to on April 10, 1952, and I understand that the enforcement of the act depends upon the designation of the regulations by the lieutenant governor in council of that province.
Should there be any way in which the federal government could assist the provinces in their legislation to protect the dairy industry from these synthetic inroads, I would ask the government that it lose no opportunity of doing so.

This title, the great wizard of Ottawa, indeed becomes the hon. Minister of Finance. Rarely have we seen so much juggling, deceit, sleight-of-hand and so forth on the part of a politician.
When I read this report, it immediately came to my mind that a Blackstone, for example, had nothing on the Minister of Finance.

Blackstone has us believe that he has just sawn a woman in two, even though the woman is still alive, while the Minister of Finance, pretending to lop off most of our taxes, hardly scratches them at all. From a single cone of paper, Blackstone draws a lot of multicoloured handkerchiefs-

speechtext:
Very nice colours. From very little taxation relief, the Minister of
The Budget-Mr. Courtemanche Finance wishes to give the illusion that he is granting everybody drastic tax reductions.
Harry Blackstone is certainly an ace at sleight-of-hand but however great he may be as a magician, he must sometimes recognize that he is powerless when faced with the simplest things.
Last January, he was in a New York city hotel with his wife, when she told him that her favourite hamster Poncho had disappeared from the suite she occupied and that searches on the whole floor had been fruitless.
In spite of Mr. Blackstone's magic words "hocus pocus", his mysterious gestures and the weirdest invocations, Poncho could not be found. He had to admit to newspapermen that he, Harry Blackstone, who could make elephants vanish and come back several years later, was absolutely powerless to locate the little rather harmless rodent which was as dear to his wife as a precious piece of jewelry.
Our great wizard at Ottawa, to use a phrase coined by the Daily Mirror, has just had an adventure somewhat similar to his distinguished colleague Blackstone.
Our Minister of Finance has cut taxes here and there by the million-at least, he has tried to give that impression-but he has been unable to alleviate, in any noticeable measure, the tax burden of the head of the family, the worker, the farmer, in a word, of the taxpayer of average or below average means.
From the gallery, the federal wizard may have seemed to do tremendous, colossal, fantastic wonders, but for the needy, for those who most deserved real and authentic tax reductions, the wizard has done nothing worth-while. One would look in vain throughout that budget for something that might bring comfort to the father or mother of a family. The family has been completely ignored and overlooked. Who will benefit from those tax reductions? Those with considerable earnings, and nobody else. Consequently, don't be surprised to hear what I heard during the last few days in my riding, that it is a rich man's budget.
In any event these are more or less the terms used by the leader of the Canadian Congress of Labour, an association with 370,000 members, I am told. According to a Canadian Press despatch, published in the newspaper La Presse, of Montreal, on February 21, 1953, the Congress had this to say about the budget:
Canadian workers will be quite disappointed in this budget which Mr. Abbott has incorrectly called a social dividend budget, whereas, in fact, it is a
2456	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Courtemanche financial dividend budget. The latest figures published by the dominion bureau of statistics show that 75 per cent of heads of families have a revenue of less than $3,000. The new income tax scale means a savings of $5 a year for the married workers whose revenue is $2,500. If he has two children, the new budget means a savings of $2 for the year 1953.	"
In his review of the economic position of Canada, Mr. Abbott gives the Canadian worker credit for the increase in Canadian production. His budget is a strange kind of reward for them.
Mr. Abbott had about $260,000,000 to distribute and he distributed this amount almost entirely to those who were not the most deserving.
He has reduced by $97,000,000 the corporation income tax and this reduction is retroactive to January 1. He has reduced by about $100,000,000 the personal income tax, but this reduction will be put into effect only on July 1. Moreover, as far as personal income tax is concerned, it is wealthy taxpayers who are granted the most substantial reductions.
Contrary to what happens in the case of the small wage earners, the taxpayer who earns $50,000 a year is granted a reduction of $1,200, whether he has children or not. If his income is $100,000, he will benefit from a reduction of more than $3,000.
The government's main excuse for not undertaking a health insurance program was that it could not afford it. But it can afford giving away $97,000,000 to corporations and granting substantial income tax reductions to wealthy taxpayers. Mr. Abbott said again and again that he could not do any more for the underdeveloped countries because he would have had to increase taxes.
Now he makes tax concessions, particularly to the rich, to the tune of more than $250 million. He could have left untouched the corporation tax and he could have given about $100 million to the backward countries and still have more than $150 million to lighten the tax burden of those in the lower income brackets.
I want to consider tor a moment the main items of the budget we are now discussing and find out what relief it gives to the little fellow, to the average taxpayer.
The Canadian Congress of Labour has shown that the income tax reductions were insignificant for the great majority of taxpayers. Nobody will question that.
The 11 per cent reduction is far from sufficient and the Minister of Finance did not even want us to benefit by the whole percentage this year. The reduction will come into effect on July 1 only, which means that in 1953 the relief will be less than 6 per cent.
Let us consider the case of a married man with two children, whose annual salary is $3,000; his wife will have to pinch and scrape every cent in order to feed and dress the family. I put the accent on the wife, for in most homes it is she who bears the brunt of a scandalous fiscal burden. What do we see 

then, in the case we are considering? The father of two children, who in the best of circumstances will scarcely be able to make both ends meet, and who, should a rainy day come, will run hopelessly into debt, will be granted a measly reduction of $7 for the whole year! It is obvious that the government is not bleeding itself white for that particular taxpayer. Moreover, the government does not bleed itself white in order to help the taxpayers earning less than. $75 or $80 per week.
The decrease in the income tax rate is, actually, only a deceit of the great wizard of Ottawa, as the Daily Mirror calls him.
It is a known fact that the personal income tax is disheartening to the workers; they cannot save anything and they have to put up with unnecessary and intolerable hardship.
I am the first to recognize that organizations like our chambers of commerce are right in asking for a somewhat fairer taxation.
Nevertheless, I feel that the income tax is a greater menace to the family than the corporation income tax is to private enterprise. And it seems to me, it would have been only logical to do something for the small wage earners, for the worker with an average income-and I mean something worth while-before granting any reductions to business.
When we blame our friends to the right for their attitude toward the family, they usually reply that there are the family allowances. Yes, family allowances do exist, but the same goes for taxes, taxes of all kinds which were unheard of when family allowances were unknown. It is becoming rather irritating for the family to always be reminded that it is receiving allowances when it dares ask for justice.
Family allowances, considering especially the rates at which they are maintained, serve only to pay taxes-income tax, federal sales tax, etc. What prevents the government from increasing these allowances to take care of the rise in the cost of living which has taken place over the last ten years?

The federal income tax is wrongly distributed; the poorest of our Canadian citizens are called upon to pay far too much in relation to their income and their family obligations.
Just consider: a gift of $7 for 1953, for the head of a family, with two dependent children, whose earnings are less than $60 a week. Is it not rather a huge joke?
Take another item, the 4 cent reduction on 20 cigarettes. It would seem that the opposition was right in saying "the higher the tax on cigarettes the lower the revenue from that source". Figures now show that everything has its day. There comes a time indeed when taxation is so high that the taxpayer seeks to elude it. He stops smoking or smokes less, or yielding to temptation, he smokes cigarettes smuggled from the United States. This 4 cent reduction on a pack of 20 cigarettes will not end smuggling. Those who have got into the habit of smoking American cigarettes will not stop because of this four cent reduction. I am not saying they are right in doing so. However, they have grown into a habit which they will lose only when the Canadian government makes it cheaper to smoke Canadian cigarettes than American cigarettes.
That situation arose because one day the government decided to overtax the people. Today, the consequences of this overtaxation are serious from the financial point of view, but even more so when we consider that people have taken to the habit of violating the law.
To sum up, the average taxpayer does not stand to benefit greatly from the lowering of the tax on cigarettes.
Corporation taxes will be reduced by approximately $120 million per year. We cannot blame the working man when, through the Canadian Congress of Labour for instance, he voices his surprise at the news that this exemption comes into effect on January 1 of the current year, while the personal income tax will be reduced only on July 1 next.
I admit that corporations, like individuals, need some relief from their taxation burden. I repeat, however, that it would have been better to think of the latter before thinking of the former. There are surely more
The Budget-Mr. Courtemanche tragic cases among individuals than among corporations.
Now what about the yearly $2.50 radio licence fee that has been abolished? This tax has always been considered a joke and an unfair tax. It was a joke because most people succeeded in avoiding it. It was unfair, because it was iniquitous to levy such a tax on the owner of a small radio. God knows, besides, how much it cost to collect that nuisance tax. Many other means will surely be found to provide the C.B.C. with all the money it needs, including money it could do without. And we shall go on paying for the C.B.C., for radio, television, shortwave service and so on and so forth. In fact, that item does not benefit the taxpayer, even the one who had to pay the $2.50 licence fee.
